Notably, our findings suggest that younger Be-type stars, specifically those with masses exceeding 10 solar masses, tend to display stronger hydrogen emission and exhibit rotation periods closer to their critical levels. Additionally, we discovered that the nebula's Be-type stars possess rotational velocities significantly lower than their maximum allowed speed, averaging 40% of it, and display non-uniform distribution of accretion in the disk. Our estimated mean age of the nebula's Be-type stars, around 4.5 million years, indicates that nebula's age is consistent with other 30 Doradus population age assessments.

Inverse Text Standardization is a crucial NLP task that converts informal text into a standardized format. The effectiveness of NLP models depends on a supply of labeled data, which is often scarce in certain language domains. To address this, data augmentation has emerged as a promising approach to enhance the models' ability to generalize. This study evaluates data augmentation techniques in data-driven NLP domains through, first, a comprehensive, cross-lingual evaluation of existing methods on standard ITZ datasets from Twitter and the 19th NIST datasets. The results indicate that context-based augmentation techniques perform well, with some achieving up to a 3.1% improvement in F1 score. The second part of our research focuses on improving data-driven NLP domains by leveraging enhanced augmentation techniques on an in-domain NLP task, specifically, the conversion of Twitter text to 19th-century English. The created dataset, "Twitter Shakespeare," will be made available to the research community.
This research explores the Faber-Krahn inequality for the eigenvalues of the Hermite operator when subject to the Robin boundary condition, and investigates the associated symmetrization method.

The success of Krieger et al. in 2019 was built upon the assumption that data across multiple domains could be effectively grouped according to their origin, and this grouping could be accurately captured by the structure of the structure-of-covariance-kernel (SCK). However, this kernel relies heavily on the assumption that data from different domains are exchangeable, and this is not always the case in real-world scenarios. In cases where data exchangeability is compromised, the SCK fails to reflect the true data grouping structure. To address this limitation, a new approach is proposed, and for two-task settings, this new approach is formalized through the concept of non-exchangeable tangent kernels (NTKs). These NTKs offer a computationally efficient solution, and their performance is evaluated against various other kernel types and the SCK across multiple binary and multi-class classification tasks.

For the first time, we demonstrate that correlations can reduce the topological structure of non-Hermitian systems with one spatial dimension. We use the winding number and spectrum generating operator, which rely on non-Hermitian counterparts, to analyze our findings. We establish that these approaches are equivalent when applied to systems with local interactions. We provide an analytical solution for a model involving two sites that incorporates non-biorthogonal eigenstates, and demonstrate the reduction of non-Hermitian topology via a correlation-induced mechanism. This phenomenon is experimentally feasible with quantum simulators based on quantum optics and quantum gases.

A person's social speaking style is a fundamental aspect of their voice identity. The current research explores how to incorporate an individual's social speaking style into synthetic speech. The experiment involved 14 adult participants, who each trained a model of their voice using about 10 minutes of speech data. The participants also provided a short text description of their speaking style and were then asked to read a passage while researchers recorded their voice. The descriptions were used by both human and machine listeners to identify whether the synthetic speech matched the speaker's voice and to rate the accuracy of the descriptions. The results show that humans can easily identify a speaker based on a short 10-second audio clip. The descriptions provided a moderate level of accuracy in identifying the speaker, but were more crucial in describing the speaker's voice characteristics. The synthetic speech matched the recorded audio sample in almost all cases. However, the descriptions provided by the speakers were not always accurate in describing their voice. The accuracy of the descriptions decreased as the length of the audio sample increased. The results also show that the synthetic speech maintained a degree of consistency with other speakers, using a standard scale to rate different voice characteristics.

A U(1) B-L symmetry is implemented to safeguard the dark matter from decay, while A4 symmetry is utilized to decompose the neutrino mass and mixing matrix, resulting in a LMA-LOW solution. Introducing a negative, radiatively generated A4 potential term allows for the inclusion of the direct detection channel of luminous dark matter, which interacts with the heat bath via the gauged B-L symmetry. This framework offers a well-justified, well-motivated A4 dark matter model that features heat-bath luminous properties.

Building on a previous study that applied the finite temperature density dependent effective potential to the Bohr-Mottola model for axially symmetric nuclei, we extend its findings by incorporating the effects of minimal length principle into the folding potential. Extending the scope, we now apply the same method to the Hamiltonian developed by Green and Malfatti for triaxial nuclei that includes the influence of minimal length principle. We then analyze the results for finite temperature and compare them to existing data. For the latter, we investigate the effect of triaxiality on the first two and three low-lying states in $^{186}$Os.

This paper explores Golay complementary sets (GCS), a generalization of Clark's Complementary Basic Sets (CBS). The paper details the creation of GCS through various methods, including the direct method, p(x)w(x) method, sequence convolution method, and polynomial method. Notably, it focuses on Neugebauer and Neumann's HCS method, which is based on CBS using the decimation technique. A significant finding is presented: a specific HCS can be created using two pairs of complementary bases over finite fields of respective sizes 3 and 5. Additionally, the paper examines Creations of GCS over finite fields of size 5 using the sequence convolution method and presents new CGS methods over finite fields of size 7, 11, and 31.

In this study, we introduce a cutting-edge technique utilizing a deep convolutional neural network autoencoder to identify alterations in complex hyperspectral images. The proposed method involves a novel, multi-stage system that integrates features from multiple layers of a autoencoder, which then condenses the data and detects changes. By representing the images with low-dimensional components, we can isolate and filter out irrelevant information and efficiently remove image noise, ultimately leading to an improved change detection performance. Experimental results using three hyperspectral datasets demonstrate the technique's capability in accurately capturing subtle alterations within rich spectral data, achieving performance levels comparable to current unsupervised change detection methods for hyperspectral images.

A relation is identified between viscosity in supercooled liquids and their residual entropy for a range of diverse molecular models. Notably, a comparison with entropic theories of viscosity is unsuccessful, suggesting a more complex connection. Subsequently, a theoretical explanation is proposed for this correlation, drawing parallels to a relation between viscosity and configurational entropy's temperature derivative discovered for Lennard-Jones spheres. Lastly, the residual entropy approach is compared with an alternative, the Stokes-Einstein-Debye equation, utilizing the configurational viscosity concept, to estimate the diffusion and rotational relaxation times in liquids composed of spherical particles with embedded dipoles.

The $\Lambda CDM$ cosmological model has traditionally viewed the universe as static. However, recent research suggests a different universe model involving cyclical patterns, which could indicate that this model may also apply to the cosmos. The acceleration of the universe's expansion might not be due to dark energy but rather the beginning of a cyclical pattern, based on a cycle that occurred over 13.8 billion years ago.

The Invariant-set hypothesis, proposed by Conley and Smith, suggests that the set of points governing quantum events operates within a higher-dimensional superdeterministic hidden-variable system. This paper evaluates the Invariant-set hypothesis by analyzing the behavior of three systems: a point remaining stationary, an object moving at a constant speed in one dimension, and a simple experiment resembling John Bell's theoretical test. Through this analysis, the study finds that the set of points influencing the experiment behaves dynamically, moving at a constant speed in a direction perpendicular to its motion in a higher-dimensional space, contrary to the original hypothesis. This contradicts the idea that this set of points remains unchanged over time. This contradiction indicates that the superdeterministic hidden-variable framework that the Conley-Smith theory relies on is flawed.

Incorporating Neural Networks for Keyphrase Detection on the Edge of IoT Devices
This research focuses on developing a lightweight, decentralized method to detect key phrases using iot devices. Utilizing an autoencoder with an attention mechanism allows for effective representation of variable-length key phrases, which in turn facilitates enhanced large-scale keyphrase monitoring. By leveraging this approach, we can identify anomalies in individual or collective flows and reduce channel congestion. By training on local data and pruning the autoencoder, keyphrase monitoring can be performed on resource-constrained devices. Additionally, this approach can be extended to collaborative learning across devices, allowing for monitoring of global keyphrase patterns while preserving local privacy.

This research explores the connection between Fermi liquid theory in quantum field theory and statistical mechanics of non-interacting holomorphic functions, specifically within 2D complex fields. It demonstrates a gauge-covariant extension of the isomorphism between 2D massless Dirac fermions and holomorphic flows, which holds for any non-trivial background gauge field. Additionally, the study reveals a correspondence between gauge-invariant fermion properties and the phases of gauge-covariant flow fields, ultimately linking these to the non-Abelian Anyon theory.

The Group Lasso method, an extension of the Lasso for structured sparse data, has two major limitations: it's ineffective for categorical data and converges slowly in high-dimensional cases. To overcome these issues, we've created the Soft Group Lasso, which utilizes a new group penalty that can handle nominal data, and has been shown to improve convergence while maintaining strong performance. Our experiments demonstrate that this new approach outperforms Group Lasso and Sparsenet, sparsely encodes categorical data, and has a faster convergence rate in high-dimensional settings.

System designers for embedded real-time systems face a significant challenge in meeting the diverse requirements of modern systems that need to be secure, resilient, and meet real-time deadlines. To address these requirements, researchers have proposed Multiple-Granularity Importance Scaling (MGIS) Scheduling, which allows different tasks to contribute to overall system performance according to their importance rather than meet deadlines rigidly. This paper introduces a new embedded real-time operating system, T-Visor, which supports the dynamic reconfiguration of task priorities in response to changing system demands. T-Visor uses hardware-assisted virtualization to provide several key services to the Linux-based upper virtual machine, including efficient Mixed Importance task scheduling, Real-Time preemptive capabilities, and ensure Deadlines are met. Through system evaluation, we demonstrate that T-Visor can outperform existing solutions by meeting more deadlines while maintaining the same level of completion for tasks with variable priorities.

When taking a panoramic image, a common issue arises from the camera's movement, often resulting in a non-minimal, wide-angle view. Focusing on a scene's geometric structure, particularly when the camera rotates around a central point, allows for the determination of minimal answers – a key parameter in selecting the optimal camera field of view for stitching images together. However, a central movement can cause the camera to deviate from its central point, causing problems with image stitching. In this context, a new approach is proposed where the camera rotates around its optical center while also translating in the x and y directions. A geometric model based on this movement pattern allows for the development of a method to calculate the minimal field of view for stitching images, even when the camera deviates from a perfect circular path. When the camera deviates from its ideal path, a camera pose optimization algorithm is used to determine the optimal field of view for stitching images, minimizing image distortion and overlap errors.

Chimeric states arise in networks of nonlinear systems with symmetry, resulting from a mix of synchronized and desynchronized groups.  Currently, these states are observed in networks with homogeneous or a few distinct system types.  However, these properties can be relaxed, and we investigate the effect of gradually changing system parameters on chimeras.  We find that smooth parameter changes do not affect stability of chimeric states in two-group networks and that these states retain stability even after a full parameter range change.  As a result, two system types can exchange components while maintaining synchrony and desynchrony respectively.  Conversely, abrupt parameter changes may impact stability, and we explore conditions required to enter or exit chimeric states in this context.

In this study, we address the issue of controlling a linear system with unknown parameters to achieve a stable and reliable outcome, even in the face of uncertainty. Our proposed solution utilizes a modified version of Least-Squares Policy Iteration to determine the optimal control strategy. This solution is backed by theoretical analysis demonstrating its ability to guarantee convergence to a theoretically optimal strategy as more data is collected. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the method learns a control strategy that remains robust and reliable over time. Compared to other solution methods, our approach offers theoretical guarantees on reliability and is shown to outperform the industry-standard model-free Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient algorithm.

A multi-layer diagram is defined as an infinite sequence of commutative rings indexed by integers, with maps between adjacent rings forming pushout squares. We derive conditions to establish that the map from a given layer to its immediate higher layer forms an h-equivalence. A sufficient condition for this involves maps being h-equivalent on h-localized rings. We explore the impact of this diagram structure on the slice $\pi_0$ of a given layer, demonstrating that it is an h-localization of a specific algebraic structure formed from the $\pi_0$ of adjacent rings. Additionally, we prove that slice $\pi_n$ of a given layer is trivial, specifically for n greater than or equal to 5, under the given conditions. We also extend the multi-layer diagram to the context of non-commutative $\mathcal{O}$-algebras over SLH spectra, with maps between adjacent layers forming Cartesian squares, and investigate its properties and an extension to the context of DG categories.

We introduce an entropy measure in unitary random circuits that captures the behavior of entanglement reverting to its original state after being diverted by boundary impurities in the bulk entanglement entropy. In U(2) and U(3) random circuits, we observe that this entropy measure reverts to maximal entropy after a specific time frame. In the context of chaotic systems in the planar limit, this entropy measure follows the geodesic reflection principle in the spacetime diagram. Additionally, we establish that for unitary circuits with a Hamiltonian, this entropy measure's return time corresponds to the refracted entropy in Weyl tensor networks, following a geodesic path in the Weyl-Chern-Simons theory.

We introduce a general approach for extracting erasable information from stochastic systems, encompassing neural networks and real-world phenomena like animal social hierarchies and ecological relationships between predators and prey. This method allows for the tracking of information dynamics across time, revealing how information changes as it's passed down through cellular processes and the development of animals, as well as the emergence of complex systems like social hierarchies and 1D catenary systems in physics. The proposed approach offers an alternative to traditional information theories, which typically focus on the flow of information in one-way systems like communication channels.

This paper focuses on exploring invariant sets of pullbacks derived from a 3D generalized Hénon map with specific nonlinearity and given parameters. We investigate the map's behavior in relation to hyperbolic invariant sets, and demonstrate how these become invariant under pullback conditions with the right choice of map parameters. Moreover, the study aims to fill a knowledge gap regarding the existence of certain types of invariant sets in this context, and to illustrate examples of such existences using visualizations.

A key element in both the classical and quantum theory of gravity is holonomy, which is part of the classical action's formula and plays a significant role in the quantum theory, especially in the case of non-closed curves. This paper provides a detailed analysis of a specific aspect of holonomy related to the metric connection in Riemannian geometry, which is often considered complex and counterintuitive. Despite these challenges, we prove that this holonomy can be calculated practically using a calculator and a basic version of numerical integration, and we discuss its key characteristics, benefits, and evidence supporting its unique nature.

We are examining facet-like distributions of specific hook shapes within $n \times 2$ and $n \times 3$ grids, whose lengths are divisible by two or three respectively. Our research provides direct evidence for the first two out of four posits in the Borodin-Chaika-Demaitre Conjecture.

The spin Larmor clock method is used to create a timer that measures tunneling time by using the Larmor precession of the tunneling electron's spin. This method is applied to different spin and energy dependent tunneling barriers and different spin coherent states of tunneling electrons are considered. It is found that the tunneling time can be accurately calculated using the Larmor clock even when barriers have different spin characteristics.

This research explores the impact of low-energy QCD on the internal structure of heavy P-wave mesons and develops a model to describe their wavefunctions. The model's outcomes are then compared to P-von P-wave charmonium and B meson parameters, revealing near-unity correlation with experimental data. The model's predictions are subsequently utilized to examine the internal twist-3 and twist-4 wavefunctions of P-wave mesons, revealing that their distribution profiles bear a strong resemblance to those of P-wave charmonium and B mesons, with peak values located at the center.

We investigate a specific configuration of Bose-Einstein condensates that employs a single spatial mode along with three different frequency components. The system's dynamics exhibit two types of nonlinear behavior - bistability and trimming. Through the application of a two-time perturbation technique, we derive conditions that enable a thorough analysis of the switching phenomenon.

We provide a detailed study of the BMS algebra, focusing on its key components, 
including the dual rotation algebra, the structure constants, and its representation 
as a Hopf algebra. Additionally, we introduce a model featuring a double soft 
photon theory with finite photon polarization, where the theory's behavior 
under large gauge transformations is explicitly demonstrated.

Over the past few years, neural networks have revolutionized computer vision tasks, with advancements in deep learning. Nonetheless, the requirement for extensive training data and computational resources has hindered their practical application in real-world settings. Moreover, conventional deep learning models struggle to adapt to new data, requiring significant recalibration. To address these challenges, neuroscientifically inspired methods have been proposed, which leverage local feature learning and inter-node connectivity. This paper introduces an innovative method for continuous adaptive learning that surpasses traditional techniques in both accuracy and resistance to catastrophic forgetting. By incorporating online learning capabilities, our method enables a network to continuously evolve and adjust its interconnections, a process informed by principles from cognitive neuroscience and synaptic dynamics. This research showcases the feasibility of developing a neural system capable of real-time continuous learning.

We define and analyze the properties of generalized geometric shapes, associated with 4-dimensional Ricci-flat metrics, and explore their relationship to the study of spinors and conformal geometry. Our investigation also involves introducing a novel measure of these shapes and examining its implications through a conceptual link to a generalized version of the Weyl signal problem. Additionally, we conduct a numerical exploration of these shapes.

In this paper, we examine a class of functions of the form $x^{l}
\overline{x}^{m}$, where $\overline{x}$ represents conjugation in $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}
/\mathbb{F}_{q}$, with $q=p^{e}\geq 2$ and $p$ is a prime number. By analyzing 
these functions, we investigate their potential to be permutation functions or 
completely permutation-resistant. Our aim is to offer comprehensive findings on 
the case when $e=1$ and $p=2$ and over non-binary cases. Furthermore, based 
on our results, we derive various binary and non-binary permutation functions 
with diverse differential properties.

The integration of artificial intelligence and healthcare is increasingly significant,
particularly in the diagnosis of diseases. A notable area of application is in
endoscopy, a procedure where a camera captures images of the digestive tract.
These images facilitate the identification of abnormalities, including intestinal
parasites. We suggest a deep belief network-based approach to automate the
classification of worms in endoscopic videos, which involves extracting and
analyzing moving intestinal segments. The results of our experiments on the
introduced dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our method. Specifically, our
method achieved a 90% accuracy in distinguishing between cases with and without
worms and an 88% accuracy in distinguishing among three distinct worm types.

This research introduces a type of non-cooperative game on a jump-diffusion model where the market characteristics are subject to changes and involves two players: an investor and a reinsurance commissioner. The focus is on a dynamic game with a limited time period, where each player aims to maximize their own benefit within the given timeframe. We assume each player can influence the probability of different market states and the intensity of news jumps. Using the maximum principle, we derive the optimal dynamic strategies for both players within the specified time frame. To obtain these open-loop strategies, we employ the coupled forward-backward stochastic differential equations and coupled jump-diffusion equations with the mean and variance inequalities. Finally, we use Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the performance of the market strategies under varying market scenarios.

This study proposes a novel flight path planning method that uses a Genetic Algorithm to achieve precision and stability. By calculating a target trajectory based on real-time position data, the proposed method optimizes flight speed and direction to maintain steady progress. Moreover, the introduced Genetic Filter significantly reduces computational time in tracking processes. By integrating Stochastic Dual Simplex Algorithm into the PIDA method, coupled with the Genetic Filter, a highly efficient and intelligent flight path solution is obtained, demonstrating superior performance over traditional backpropagation neural network-based methods in terms of both speed and accuracy.

This review focuses on the pivotal characteristics of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy, particularly within the four-momentum range below 1 GeV/$c$. Given the pronounced chiral symmetry breaking in QCD, we extensively discuss the underlying symmetries, the mass of pions, and nucleons, along with the role of the axial vector current. We also delve into pion-nucleon scattering, production, and absorption at low energies, the structure of the nucleon, and the implications of the axial vector current. The review heavily relies on the QCD low-energy effective theory of pions and nucleons, the dispersive framework, and the QCD sum rules.

Building a comprehensive pixel detector for the Large Hadron Collider involves constructing multiple layers of readout electronics and sensors across a significant area. The CMS detector incorporates a layer of time-multiplexed pseudoradiation sensors located near the endcap region, which was initially designed for commissioning and testing purposes. This research aims to evaluate the performance of the CMS Phase-1 pixel detector edge module, focusing on the implementation of a new three-dimensional clustering algorithm that accounts for edge hit patterns and a related track-based validation technique. By analyzing proton-proton collision data, we found that the new three-dimensional algorithm effectively recovers hit patterns across both well-instrumented regions and the more complex edge areas, while also showing that the CMS edge module aligns with simulation predictions and a established CMS pixel detector validation model.

We have developed a method to categorify the shapes of AGN host galaxies identified in the HSC-WSS, utilizing their morphological characteristics. By employing the $G_{\mathrm{r}}$ parameter, which is derived from the Sersic index and axis ratio, as a proxy for galaxy shape, we are able to explore how AGN hosts are distributed. To determine the typical shape of AGN host galaxies at various redshifts, we used the $G_{\mathrm{r}}$ distribution, taking into account the effects of photometric redshift uncertainty. Furthermore, by combining HSC-WSS AGN data with literature data on host shapes, we are able to examine the correlation between AGN shape and other properties, such as AGN spectral type, as well as host mass and spin. Our findings reveal that the host $G_{\mathrm{r}}$ distribution of $z<1$ AGNs is consistent with previous studies, and also that the average host $G_{\mathrm{r}}$ increases with photometric redshift. Additionally, we found a correlation between the host $G_{\mathrm{r}}$ and AGN spectral type, and also between the host $G_{\mathrm{r}}$ and AGN host mass.

Atomic short-range correlations are investigated within a momentum and coordinate space framework. The momentum distribution function, which is widely used, is extended to a phase-space distribution through a wave-number space transformation, leveraging the Wigner transformation. This new approach enables the study of these correlations' spatial characteristics. The momentum distribution function reveals long-range symmetry but also exposes the non-trivial nature of atomic short-range correlations via its momentum structure. Consequently, the phase-space distribution exhibits distinct spatial features near the momentum origin, which vary significantly with atom type. The momentum and phase-space distributions exhibit similarities in shape, yet their scales differ. Furthermore, a correlation length, which is well-established in coordinate space, can be defined in momentum space. This novel approach to studying short-range correlations in atomic systems offers a pathway for future atomic distribution analysis.

Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in processing intricate complex data such as images, sound waves, and financial market predictions. However, the current deep learning frameworks are primarily designed for real-valued operations, necessitating the addition of a co-domain equality function to achieve exact complex results and minimize information loss. This paper presents a comprehensive study of co-domain equality in deep learning, including its implementation details, sensitivity analysis, and integration with popular complex extensions of PyTorch. The experiments demonstrate that an integrated co-domain equality can significantly enhance the performance of deep learning models for complex predictions by matching the accuracy of real-valued equivalents in solving complex problems.

The deep inelastic scattering process has served as an essential tool for studying quantum chromodynamics in the presence of large momentum transfers, initially within the context of the parton model and subsequently in the context of the Balitsky-Friedberg-Lipatov-Gribov (BFG-L) framework. At early stages, linear evolution equations with a saturation momentum power were discovered in the proton structure function, signaling saturation effects. As evolution progresses, nonlinear saturation phenomena become more pronounced, ultimately dominating proton structure functions at sufficiently high energies. Furthermore, a scaling law emerges at asymptotic limits, attributed to saturation effects. Similarly, a conical jet production process exhibits geometric scaling at the asymptotic energy limit, with scaling appearing in the proton-nucleon cross-section through the exponent of the transverse momentum.

The variation in chemical compositions among low-metallicity stars in the Milky Way's halo is significant, and researchers are still trying to understand its origins. A 2D model of neutron star mergers was used to simulate element distributions in galaxies with varying metallicities, and the results showed uniform abundance patterns at higher metallicity, but strong abundance variations at lower metallicity. This suggests variations in alpha elements and iron group elements at low metallicity, but not in r-process elements. These findings are consistent with observations of the globular cluster $\omega$ Centauri, indicating the need to consider multiple origins of both neutron star mergers and the metallicity variations within the cluster.

This research introduces a comprehensive framework for measuring how sensitive machine learning models are to changes in input data. We apply this framework to predict scores for an educational assessment, using diverse features such as a student's demographic information, reading ability, and prior test results. By employing various machine learning techniques, our analysis assesses their effectiveness in identifying and using sensitive features. Additionally, our framework incorporates multiple sensitivity metrics and methods, including machine learning models, perturbation analysis, and Bayesian interpretation, to validate the results. Our study ultimately ranks our framework's predictions against those made by machine learning models, demonstrating their reliability and accuracy. By open-sourcing our framework, we enable the scientific community to utilize it for assessing the fairness of machine learning models.

This paper explores the integration of SQUID amplifiers in Quantum Computing, specifically within Microwave Quantum Computing using superconducting circuits. As an extremely sensitive amplifier of extremely weak microwave signals, SQUIDs play a pivotal role in this type of computing. However, their application is often overlooked. By incorporating SQUIDs, the detection and readout processes can be significantly improved. We examine the SQUID's functioning and introduce a method forSQUID learning, identifying key indicators that signify the SQUID's readiness for reliable quantum computing operations. Ultimately, SQUID learning can be used to fine-tune the SQUID for optimal performance.

Two novel distorted product structures have been proposed, followed by conditions for 
a submanifold to be classified as distorted product semi-isotropic, semi-minimal, or
isotropic within a nearly contact manifold. Research is also conducted on
a distorted product nearly contact submanifold with a pointwise semi-slant structure, 
establishing when such a submanifold can be considered distorted product pointwise semi-slant. 
Examples are also provided to illustrate these findings.

A significant hurdle in low energy nuclear research, specifically nuclear recoil detection, lies in accurately distinguishing between inoperative nuclear events and operative ones. This research examines the potential of using nanoscale amorphous carbon inorganic inclusions within a single crystal of diamond to identify and analyze inactive nuclear recoil occurrences. The inclusions within this type of diamond act as centers that emit light in response to mechanical stress, making them suitable for detecting such events. By combining high-resolution light detection with precise location tracking using optical microscopy, the inclusions' reactive states can be modified, allowing researchers to differentiate between operative and inactive nuclear recoil occurrences. This new inoperative nuclear recoil examination tool, named PALEOCCENE, is introduced and its capabilities are demonstrated through the analysis of silicon ion impacts.

We explore the movement of a particle within an uneven distribution of energy across its environment, where energy is introduced by the collision with other non-interacting particles, each having a specific probability of returning the energy to the particle, reducing over time, and its excess energy dissipates at a different rate. We derive an analytical solution for the position of the particle over time, find that, on average, it moves in a direction opposite to the increasing energy, where it slows down and settles when its energy is, on average, lowest, where it also moves in a straight line, as verified by computer simulation, and find that, when energy dissipates very quickly, the movement of the particle is similar to that of a Brownian motion, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line, where it also moves in a straight line,

The fractional quantum Hall effect exhibits distinct magnetorotons, which are collective excitations crucial in understanding its characteristics. Researchers have long assumed a single magnetoroton exists per fraction, based on prior numerical and experimental findings. However, recent research has challenged this assumption, particularly after discovering a mode exhibiting spectral total regulation at specific fractions like 5/2 and 7/2. This phenomenon suggests the presence of multiple magnetorotons, each exhibiting spectral total regulation, rather than just one, as seen in other Hall systems. To explore this idea, we studied spectral totals at various fractions and found the presence of multiple magnetorotons in systems like 3/4, 5/8, 7/8, 9/10, 11/10, 13/10, and 13/8. This research provides insight into the unique nature of fractional quantum Hall effect.

Identifying and analyzing clusters of connected nodes with node failures, such as in networks, is crucial for understanding phenomena such as the spread of diseases or computer network security. In our research, we developed an efficient algorithm for identifying clusters in complex networks where nodes are connected and node failures are represented by their respective weights. Our algorithm, based on a geometric approach, allows for the analysis of clusters in large-scale networks, with applications in epidemiology and network security. Specifically, we tested our algorithm on networks representing disease spread and found that it accurately identifies clusters of infected nodes, with implications for understanding the spread of diseases. Furthermore, we applied our algorithm to the study of the phase transitions in the percolation process, using the critical exponent for the cluster size distribution to characterize the behavior of the algorithm. Our results demonstrate that our algorithm is capable of accurately identifying clusters in networks, with implications for the understanding of epidemiological phenomena and network security.

When creating maximum likelihood maps for the Cosmic Microwave Background, the use of a fixed, square grid can inadvertently lead to spurious signals at the centers of maps and octupolar noise patterns due to symmetry breaking. Researchers have previously suggested using stochastic origin placements to mitigate this issue, but we find this approach can be overly conservative, especially in high-resolution maps where map size is the only factor influencing likelihood probabilities. We demonstrate that the likelihood probability of the true origin position, derived from high-resolution mock data, is significantly lower than that of neighboring positions, thereby reducing the likelihood of false positive signals in real data. We show that shifting map origins by as little as 0.005 degrees is sufficient to eliminate most spurious signals observed in real data, thereby minimizing computational costs for future high-resolution maps.

We examine how different goal-oriented reinforcement learning techniques handle verbal references in their training process. Our investigation involves a modified version of the Social Dilemma environment inspired by game theory, designed to assess how well RL algorithms handle multiple, conflicting verbal directives. The environment is based on a 2-agent setup, allowing us to investigate various language interpretation challenges. By implementing this framework, we found that most existing goal-oriented RL algorithms struggle to effectively navigate situations where an agent receives multiple verbal directives, highlighting a significant area of concern. To address this issue, we propose a language module inspired by referential communication theory, enabling agents to infer the meaning of verbal references. Our results demonstrate that this language module allows the agents to evolve cooperative strategies, ultimately enabling them to reach the Nash Equilibrium in the game.

Quantum process tomography is a crucial method in characterizing quantum processes. However, traditional approaches require a large number of measurements, which can be extremely time-consuming. To address this limitation, a new "shadow" based method has been developed, allowing for more efficient measurements. Specifically, for channels operating on single qubits, the shadow procedure achieves statistical accuracy comparable to conventional methods, while requiring ten times fewer measurements. Additionally, a variant of the shadow approach has been proposed for multi-qubit channels, offering improved statistical accuracy in scenarios with significant noise levels.

For a planar convex shape P, the first eigenvalue of its Dirichlet Laplacian is denoted by $\lambda_1(p)$ and the isoperimetric quotient is represented by $I(P)$. The paper derives specific inequalities relating the Cheeger constant h(P), I(P), and $\lambda_1(p)$. It proves that $h(P)$ is bounded below by $\frac{4\pi I(P)}{|\Omega|}$ and above by $\frac{4\pi I(P)^{3/2}}{|\Omega|}$, with the lower bound being an equality when I(P) equals 1. Additionally, it establishes that $h(P)$ is at least $\frac{C_0}{|\Omega|}$ and at most $\frac{C_0}{|\Omega|} \frac{I(P)}{\sqrt{I(P)}}$, with the constant C_0 being determined by the shape factor C_0 = $\min_{\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2, \text{convex}} \frac{h(P)}{|\Omega|}$. It is shown that $C_0$ is a finite, positive, shape-dependent value and that $C_0 = \frac{2}{3}$.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly being utilized for applications requiring prompt delivery, such as delivering life-saving medical supplies to areas inaccessible by traditional means. This study focuses on optimizing the delivery route for a single UAV that must complete its mission within a set timeframe. The problem is formulated as an integer programming problem, with a proposed solution method involving an initial exact approach and a heuristic approximation for larger problems. A simulation was carried out to compare the solution method's performance against random heuristics and evaluate their efficiency through runtime analysis. The results indicate that the proposed method consistently outperforms the random approach while providing a bound on solution quality for smaller problems.

The critical behavior of interaction-relevant bilayer graphene can be understood through the renormalization group analysis. Specifically, the five-body interaction term in the model's Hamiltonian becomes critically important when considering Coulomb interactions between bilayer electrons. Studies have shown that the four-body interaction term becomes stronger as energy scales decrease, leading to a point where the perturbation theory breaks down. At this point, the multiple-body interaction term takes over, necessitating a new approach to understanding the interaction-relevant bilayer graphene model.

The Sc2TbN@C80 fullerenes were studied on h-BN/Ni(111) surface, where two distinct positions were discovered through variable-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy. At low temperatures, the molecules occupied the hollow sites, and as the temperature increased, they shifted to the bridge sites. Using DFT calculations, the energy barriers for this transition were estimated to be approximately 140 meV. Additionally, the molecular conformations were analyzed in both positions, and the energy difference between them was estimated to be approximately 230 meV, aligning with experimental observations.

In the last decade, the Internet of Things (IoT) has grown into a major player in global networking, with numerous low-energy devices now capable of connecting to networks and gathering data. These devices, however, suffer from significant constraints in terms of computational power, memory, and energy, making them vulnerable when employing traditional cryptographic methods. In response, a new set of lightweight cryptographic algorithms was developed to provide a balance between security and performance. This paper will review and analyze various low-energy IoT devices, along with an in-depth examination of a range of lightweight cryptographic methods. Furthermore, it will introduce and compare several comparison criteria for evaluating these algorithms.

To determine precise physical constants or compare values, a highly sensitive and expensive device may be utilized in an adaptive, one-by-one approach, adjusting each setting based on the results of the previous measurement. This method is known as the Ramsey sequence, a technique employed in the precise timekeeping of modern atomic clocks. We have developed an algorithm to analyze adaptive Ramsey sequence data in an ever-changing process, outperforming existing methods that rely on an assumed probability distribution, especially in cases where this prior may not accurately represent available knowledge. In an experiment, we have successfully measured the magnetic field required for a specific nuclear resonance in a $^{155}$W nucleus in real-time, achieving a result that was accurate within a small margin, while also outperforming an alternative method by a significant margin.

Network centrality metrics assess node importance by measuring its connection strength to other nodes. Gromov centrality is a novel, scale-invariant metric that quantifies each edge in a network based on its network distance from the two connected nodes. The Gromov score is calculated as the difference between the Gromov distance and the two nodes' network distance. A lower score indicates more central nodes, which can create shortcuts or shortcuts in the network. The method is applied to identify evolutionarily central amino acids in proteins, which are critical for maintaining protein stability. Additionally, it can be used to identify hubs in complex networks and aid in feature engineering through network distance analysis.

This work outlines an azymuthally symmetrical theory of gravity that is composed of an energy density of a self-contained field, which is negative, along with the corresponding momentum, stress, and curvature. A static and round object is characterized by the Schwarzschild metric. A round orbit's equations are identical in form to those found in general relativity.

Building upon previous research on the classification of collections of matrices or matrix pencils under strict equivalence, this paper expands upon these findings by examining class functions on collections of matrix pencils. The study demonstrates the natural correspondences between collections, class functions, and multilinear forms, then determines the fully multiplicative class functions, class functions invariant under rigid motions, and multilinear class functions, ultimately showing their close connection to individual classes within a field of complex numbers.

We propose a geometric interpretation of T-duality for twisted tori that parallels the established concept developed in Lie groups. Our approach is rooted in a dual Lie algebra relationship and the corresponding tori associated with these groups. To justify this theory, we examine key properties such as a torus' Whitehead form, the twisted cohomology of the corresponding twisted orbifold and the twistor map. This framework is particularly versatile as it encompasses the previously described cases of R-torsion and twisted R-torsion.

We have established a bound for embedding tree-depth 2 planar metrics of size n into metrics with treewidth at most O(log^2 n). Furthermore, for any fixed subset of the plane, we have established a bound for embedding the induced metric of that subset into treewidth-bounded metrics. Specifically, we have established upper bounds of O(sqrt(n)/log^2 n) and O(sqrt(n)/log^(3/2)(n)) respectively. In addition, we have developed a general framework for embedding metric spaces derived from fixed, compact plane figures under the induced Euclidean metric. This framework enables a bound for embedding treewidth at most O(sqrt(n)/log^(3/2)(n)). Moreover, we have shown that for any fixed subset of the plane, we can embed the induced metric into treewidth at most O(sqrt(n)/log^(3/2)(n)) with distortion. In fact, we have established that this bound applies when any fixed compact plane figure is embedded into the grid metric of size n. In fact, we have shown that for any fixed compact plane figure, we can embed a subset of the grid metric of size n into treewidth at most O(sqrt(n)/log^(3/2)(n)) with distortion.

This research examines the smooth, discrete-time system $x_{k+1} = f(x_k)$ defined on a compact, differentiable manifold $M$, where the vector field $f$ is strongly monotonic with respect to a continuous order relation on $M$, and there exists an absorbing compact $M_s \subset M$. The main outcome of this study indicates that the dynamics of such systems typically exhibit a dynamic decomposition, characterized by the presence of invariant sets comprising non-wandering points and invariant sections containing half-dynamical rules, where trajectories behave similarly to random walks as they approach the boundary of these invariants, under the condition that the boundary itself constitutes a continuous invariant manifold. Additionally, specific examples demonstrate the ubiquity of the described scenario. Furthermore, this study delves into the behavior of such systems under additional assumptions, specifically when global asymptotic stability is unattainable, analyzing the asymptotic behavior of half-dynamical rules near invariant boundaries, and discussing the implications of this analysis.

The variational quantum eigensolver is a crucial method for solving the electronic Schrödinger equation using quantum computers. Its performance is significantly impacted by the choice of ansatz, which is often static and not tailored to the system at hand. In this research, we propose an ansatz that dynamically adjusts based on the system's fermionic excitations from the ground state, and we evaluate its effectiveness compared to other methods through simulations on the FermiHub problem, a challenging test case for quantum systems. The results show that our method can achieve a more accurate approximation of the Schrödinger wavefunction using fewer resources, and we also consider how quantum noise may affect the method's performance.

A novel, interpretable, and training-free decoder is introduced, leveraging a
trained neural model's internal representations to accurately decode the target
output, particularly effective in complex tasks such as image generation. By
using a machine-assisted probability distribution based on a trained model's
confidence, this decoder significantly outperforms traditional, fixed, and
neural decoders in various tasks, including complex representations, high
dimensionality, and data distribution sensitivity. Notably, it achieves excellent
results in imbalanced learning scenarios, providing a substantial foundation for
further improvements in learning and interpretation.

The Hubble tension is a pressing issue in cosmology, with its resolution potentially lying in new physics discoveries enabled by gravitational waves generated during inflation. A specific type of gravitational wave, known as the rigid-amplified (RAR) mode, is unique in its ability to leave detectable imprints on both nano-Hz and MHz bands of gravitational-wave spectra, as well as cosmic microwave background data. Our research focuses on RAR mode signatures in the NANOGrav 12th Data Release, the H0-LCDM cosmology, and a new detection of gravitational-wave signals at the MHz range using data from the ARTEMIS mission, as well as recent results from the Advanced LIGO-Virgo and cosmic microwave background experiments. The RAR mode's characteristics are found to be in agreement with observations, with the amplitude of gravitational waves at the RAR mode's peak frequency being approximately $h^*_\text{RAR}(f) \sim 10^{-10} f^{-0.5}$, where $f$ is the frequency in Hz. The RAR mode's non-Gaussian properties are also found to be in agreement with observations. The addition of RAR mode gravitational waves to the standard cosmic evolution model is found to reduce the discrepancy between H0 values from cosmic microwave background data and local measurements by the Hubble Space Telescope. The RAR mode's characteristics are found to be in agreement with observations, with the amplitude of gravitational waves at the R

PanSTARRS, a long-period comet, has been studied using the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) attached to ALMA at an altitude of 4,1000 meters above sea level. Observations were conducted in June 2016, when the comet was approximately 2.8 astronomical units away from Earth and the array was configured to detect features as small as 14 kilometers. Five molecular species were targeted in the study, including carbon monoxide, carbon monosulfide, carbon dioxide, methanol, and carbon monoxide. The results showed that water and carbon monoxide emission rates were significantly higher than expected, indicating the sublimation of volatile ices. The carbon monosulfide to water ratio was found to be unusually high, and the molecule's spatial distribution suggested a source within the comet's nucleus, as confirmed by the absence of a source in the comet's coma. The data also revealed that the comet's volatile components were not homogeneously mixed, and the carbon monoside was likely not produced by the sublimation of volatile ices.

This study introduces an unsupervised approach to creating speech without requiring text labels, significantly reducing annotation costs. The proposed method employs a text-to-speech model that operates without supervision, accompanied by speech assessment components that also function without labels. The method was tested using the MMS-880 dataset, a massive corpus of 880 speaker phrases, and demonstrated impressive results, particularly on 80 speaker phrases that were reserved as a test set and 10 new speaker phrases that were not annotated with text at all.

This article explores the effectiveness of Tsallis entropy as a strong constraint for searching for viable cosmological solutions in the context of Holographic Dark Energy. Assuming the Holographic Dark Energy acts like a form of quintessence with negative pressure, we analyze the dynamic behavior of the model and investigate its stability using the perturbation analysis method. We also consider the impact of incorporating complex modifications into the Holographic Dark Energy term and find that the model can be stable even in the presence of such modifications.

Multi-objective Mixed Integer Non Linear Optimization problems are widespread in real-world applications and often arise in real-life scenarios. The constraints and decision variables in such problems are non-linear complex equations, and they include both continuous and integer variables. Researchers have developed the Multi-Objective Branch and Bound algorithm to provide an optimal solution set for multi-objective Mixed Integer Non Linear Optimization problems. This paper proposes an enhanced version of the Branch and Bound algorithm, called the Branch and Bound Enhanced by Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II, to provide a set of non-dominated solutions for MO-MINOPs. The proposed algorithm was tested on several datasets, and it showed superior performance compared to the traditional Branch and Bound algorithm.

We demonstrate that within the framework of nonstandard differential geometry, linked Lie groupoids, which are mathematically robust, possess an intrinsic property of connectivity that is minimal. Specifically, they satisfy connectedness and integral completeness conditions, which can be characterized as the largest connected and integrable subgroupoid within the larger groupoid structure. This result relies on the duality inherent in Lie groupoids, which enables the translation of geometric properties into algebraic properties, thereby establishing a direct relationship between these concepts and the Lie algebra of the groupoid.

The 21st century's scientific advancements rely heavily on the widespread adoption of scientific data sharing. However, various legal and ethical concerns, such as intellectual property rights, data privacy, and intellectual honesty, pose significant obstacles to this goal. To overcome these barriers, numerous data sharing services have been developed, each with its own terms and conditions, which can hinder seamless data sharing between institutions, especially in fields like biomedical sciences, where large datasets are common. To address this issue, we've created an open-source cyberinfrastructure platform, CIBER, which facilitates secure data sharing between distinct data sources, each with its own terms and conditions, by allowing users to retrieve remote data via a unified gateway interface. This paper showcases CIBER's capabilities through a demo session featuring diverse cyberinfrastructure resources, including a PostgreSQL database, a virtual machine, and a cloud-based virtual machine.

In Aspect-driven Sentiment Analysis, the explicit sentiment expressed towards an aspect often remains unclear or is only partially conveyed, a phenomenon we term implicit sentiment. To address this challenge, we've developed a pre-trained, robust language model called SUPRAP, which leverages unique semantic relationships between aspects and sentiment opinions through supervised pre-training. By integrating a pre-trained model with a compact classifier, our ASPrep method effectively captures implicit sentiment. To further enhance our method, we've introduced a joint learning framework called JASP using a shared neural network that captures common sentiment representations from monosemantic aspects and distinct ones from polysemous aspects. Comprehensive evaluations across various public datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in Aspect-driven Sentiment Analysis.

We investigate methods for identifying and computing the odds ratio (OR) that operates through a binary mediator in case-control studies involving the outcome. Our research indicates the direct effect and interaction effect odds ratios can be computed using specific case-control sampling strategies. However, estimating odds ratio associated with the mediator requires a more comprehensive sample, as it is influenced by the odds ratio of the unmeasured outcome. Two specific sampling strategies are identified: complete data or two-stage sampling, which are shown to yield identifiable individual-level effects but require significant effort. Consequently, specific computation models are developed to estimate a class of computation-augmented effects under various scenarios. Two sampling models are presented: the Mediation through Probabilistic Causal Paths (MPC) and the Mediation through Joint Conditional Probabilities (JCP), which are shown to challenge conventional case-control sampling assumptions in the presence of binary mediators. Our findings are validated through Monte Carlo simulations and an analysis of real-world data.

This study proposes a robust multiuser transmission design for confidential data transfer within Ricean communication networks, incorporating reconfigurable intelligent surfaces but accounting for practical hardware limitations such as imperfect knowledge of channel conditions and errors in the generation of phase shifts. The authors derive an analytical expression for the secret rate of a multiuser system, including the effects of various hardware imperfections. The obtained results are then utilized to develop an efficient global optimization method, yielding an optimal solution to the non-convex transmission problem. The numerical analysis shows the valuable uplink capacity gained by intelligently managing the spectrum with the aid of RIS, even when considering various hardware imperfections. The authors also assess the impact of various hardware imperfections on the performance of the multiuser system and the effectiveness of the proposed reconfigurable intelligent surface-assisted transmission design.

This study proposes a value-based strategy that involves using a comparative approach to define ability as a key factor in shaping one's work experience. By employing this ability-orientated strategy, individuals can gain a renewed perspective on their career and establish a positive self-worth. A central component of this strategy is a retrospective summarization technique, which serves as a means to reframe and relabel past work experiences in a positive light. From a theoretical perspective, this strategy is grounded in self-determination theory, emphasizing the ability to take control of one's career and assert one's value. Building upon this foundation, the study outlines key ability-boosting practices that individuals can adopt to enhance their self-perceived ability and ultimately, their self-worth.

The solar breeze, a type of low-speed plasma stream, comprises material ejected from the solar wind and flows at speeds of 350-450 km/s, primarily emanating from the equatorial regions. Historically, studies of the solar breeze have primarily relied on data collected from near the solar surface, obtained through the SOHO spacecraft, and have revealed its characteristics and energy flow patterns. However, research has yet to fully understand how the solar breeze evolves as it expands and propagates through space. A new study involving data from the Parker Solar Probe, a spacecraft that has reached closer to the sun than any other, has shown that the solar breeze exhibits distinct features, including coronal holes, coronal bright regions, and wave activity, which evolve as it moves through space. A notable finding is that the solar breeze obtained from Parker Solar Probe, obtained at a distance of about 20 million km from the sun, contains more energy and magnetic fields than expected, which could indicate that it retains its original characteristics and energy flow patterns.

In a quantum context, we define a principal bundle with σ-finite fibers as having locally trivial bundles, which enables the construction of noncommutative principal bundles over compact spaces with uncountable Trakhtman groups, by leveraging action-based C*-algebra methods.

The study of cardinal characteristics in set theory has a long history, but it has only recently gained enough momentum to produce some noteworthy findings. This study delves into two specific invariants, $u$ and $nd$, which reside within the range of $(\aleph_1, 2^{\aleph_1}]$. It is demonstrated that it is consistent that $\mathfrak u$ surpasses $\mathcal{nd}$ by multiple levels without breaching any $\aleph_\omega$ threshold. Furthermore, it is shown that it is consistent that $\mathfrak u$ is strictly less than or equal to $\mathcal{nd}$. This consistency can be achieved through a combination of either Martin's Axiom or the GCH, as well as a specific forcing poset for specific GCH values.

The $q$ deformed Schrödinger-Heisenberg model in optomechanical systems is computationally efficient and adaptable, yet its methods have either been heavily shrouded in technical jargon or overly generalized, resulting in a lack of clarity. In this study, both theoretical and practical aspects of the $q$ deformed model are examined within a $q$ deformed optomechanical system. Two methods of implementing $q$ deformation are explored: one involving the de Sitter model with $q = \tanh(\xi)$ and the other the Adler model with $q = e^\xi$. Two types of optical solitons, fast and slow, are analyzed using the conserved energy model. Furthermore, the graph of clarity versus $q$ deformation for fast solitons reveals an optimal value of $\xi = 0.333$ and $q = 0.982$. Similarly, for the soliton stability, a best value of $\xi = 0.267$ and $q = 0.937$ are identified.

Within the framework of the Dual-Rotors Model, which is a type of supersymmetric model, we investigate R-parity violating interactions in the Higgs-fermion sector. These interactions arise naturally from a scenario where two rotating sectors, representing the Higgs and fermion sectors, intersect at right angles. We analyze R-parity violating mass terms and mixing angles resulting from neutral and charged Higgs-fermion interactions. We highlight that R-parity violating scissors modes can occur between neutral, chiral fermion pairs, such as electron-positron, muon-antimuon, and tau-antitau combinations. We note that the tau-antitau scissors mode is particularly significant and potentially detectable via a dipole moment. We predict that the dual-rotors mechanism can account for observed dipole moments in the electron and muon and produce visible effects at the LHC and LHCx.

A novel cell-mean based neural network (CMBNN) is introduced to tackle 1D hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations with various boundary and initial conditions. In the case of hyperbolic PDEs, the method uses a first-order finite difference scheme for time discretization and a cell-mean based spatial flux approximation. A one-step feed-forward neural network is then employed to forecast the flux. The method employs the L1 loss function and is solvable via an efficient gradient descent algorithm. The technique is adaptive and relies on local data, enabling its use in parallel for time-marching PDE solutions. Furthermore, it can handle discontinuous solutions and is capable of capturing shocks. The proposed approach demonstrates robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods in computational speed while maintaining or exceeding accuracy levels.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC is focused on investigating the properties of the quark-gluon plasma and other extreme conditions. It also studies fixed nucleon interactions and small collision systems such as p-Pb and Xe-Pb, in addition to studying quarkonium regeneration and the spin structure of the proton. The experiment will enhance its capabilities beyond LHC Run 3, primarily by integrating a high-granularity electromagnetic calorimeter, a Resistive Plate Chamber, and other upgrades to its muon system, central detectors, and roman pots. These improvements will significantly extend the experiment's reach in luminosity and transverse momentum, thereby increasing its sensitivity to various physical processes, including rare ones. The upgraded system will also be able to investigate new states of matter formed in heavy-ions and small-systems collisions, as well as further enhance the experiment's roman pots capabilities.

Our study introduces a timelike Unruh effect, a phenomenon where entanglement is shared between a particle and its antiparticle, but separated by the event horizon instead of space. This new effect is grounded in the old, spacelike Unruh effect's principles. This effect gives rise to a geometric phase in the particle's wave function, which varies in proportion to the timelike angle formed by the past event horizon. This effect can be verified experimentally, thereby validating the new unruh effect's existence.

Event extraction is a crucial task in Natural Language Processing that involves identifying and structuring real-world events from text. Although there have been significant advancements in English event extraction, there is still a substantial need for progress in supporting multilingual and diverse contextual features. This study introduces a new multilingual dataset, named MEE, which spans 14 languages and includes over 200,000 articles along with more than 1.2 million event excerpts and over 2.5 million entity pairs. Our proposed multilayer model leverages the MEE dataset to achieve state-of-the-art results in both multilingual and contextual feature extraction tasks.

Our analysis examines the correlation between X-ray timing properties and spectral characteristics in an accreting black hole, specifically focusing on the system Cyg X-1 during its hard state operation. We utilize a multi-wavelength dataset collected over 103.6 days to investigate relationships among the Poisson fluctuation parameters, the harmonic amplitude, the k-alpha parameter, and various temperature parameters. We identify two distinct groups, characterized by distinct spectral characteristics and temporal behaviors. Group A features lower hardness and higher photon energy rates, along with the dominance of disk blackbody radiation. The soft-interval transfer function and soft photons produced by the stellar breeze predominantly influence the soft X-ray band in group A. In contrast, group B has the dominance of a power-law component and the participation of the stellar breeze and hard X-ray corona as primary contributors to soft and hard X-ray bands, respectively. The soft-interval transfer function and the hard corona's intrinsic temporal variability and geometric characteristics play a significant role in the soft-interval and hard-interval, respectively. Our findings suggest that two distinct regimes exist in Cyg X-1, driven by the interplay between soft-interval transfer function and hard corona variability.

The study of a specific ether-like modification of four-dimensional abelian gauge theory is carried out, incorporating the principle of gauge invariant. By expanding on work by Bergshoeff, Halverson, and 't Hooft, three distinct static gauge configurations are obtained, each influenced by temperature. When the temperature is not zero, the gauge theory's Lagrangian is temperature-dependent, allowing for the calculation of the theory's partition function, energy, and entropy.

This proposal outlines a plan for a cooperative task aimed at enhancing the capabilities of the SWALLANG Natural Language Processing (NLP) toolkit, with a focus on breaking the current separation between syntactic and semantic analysis modules. The goal is to integrate a shared computational platform, leveraging shared resources such as data, models, and computing power to improve efficiency and cross-use. The project will begin by analyzing the dependencies among syntactic and semantic features to identify optimal collaborative strategies, followed by the development of a iterative feature engineering process to optimize performance through shared resource allocation and analysis.

The observation of binary neutron star mergers has sparked interest in the potential for these events to generate short gamma-ray bursts (Blobs or SPBs) via the accretion disk. By simulating the interaction of magnetized accretion disks with the surrounding supernova ejecta, researchers discovered that the disk's magnetic field can trigger a more intense ejection of material, resulting in an observable gamma-ray burst. The simulations showed that the most intense ejections, capable of producing SPBs, occur when the disk's mass is at least 0.1 solar masses and the initial magnetic field strength is around 10^-6 to 10^-7 Tesla. The results suggest that the disk is the primary source of Ejections in the case of equal-mass mergers with low kick velocities, while the material is typically generated by the disk in mergers with low kick velocities. The simulations also reveal that the disk's magnetic field can be amplified to produce the required energy for the Ejections. The team plans to further investigate the complex interplay between the disk, the ejecta, and the surrounding environment to better understand the origin of the Ejections.

A comprehensive, large-scale survey is being conducted to identify and quantify the effects of tidal features in early-type galaxies across the local universe. By utilizing the Hyper Suprime-Cam on the Subaru Telescope, we have obtained wide-field imaging data to determine the proportion of tidal features in the luminosity of galaxies within a specific magnitude range. By examining galaxies with magnitudes between -17.5 and -14.5, we have identified the typical fractions of their luminosities contained within tidal features. Our analysis reveals that blue tidal features constitute approximately 0.4% of the luminosity of all galaxies, 1.2% of disk galaxies, 2.4% of galaxies with prominent bars, and 7.2% of galaxies without bars. In contrast, red tidal features account for about 0.9% of the luminosity of all galaxies, 0.6% of disk galaxies, 0.6% of galaxies with prominent bars, and 1.2% of galaxies without bars. Utilizing these findings, we have estimated the mass fractioning efficiency of tidal features to be approximately 0.015 per galaxy per year, indicating that galaxies with bars form slightly more efficiently than those without bars. Our study also highlights the importance of including all galaxies, not just those with mergers, in models of tidal feature formation.

A new phenomenon known as "repellent gravitation" is explored in an azimuthally symmetric framework. In an experimental study conducted in a laboratory, bipolar electromagnetic jets were observed to be expelled from the surface of various charge carriers, such as water droplets and gas bubbles. This phenomenon, attributed to the intense electrostatic forces at play, serves as a model for understanding similar but astronomically larger entities, namely bipolar stellar jets. In an effort to replicate the stellar phenomenon in a laboratory setting, researchers employed large charged water droplets and gas bubbles as analogues for stars, while bipolar electromagnetic jets were treated as representations of bipolar stellar jets. By measuring the repulsive forces at play, researchers were able to quantify the mass equivalent of these ultralight objects, revealing an intriguing connection between the mass of an object, its electric charge, and its radius. Researchers propose that the repulsive effect originates from the intense electric fields at the object's surface, an effect that becomes increasingly pronounced as the object's surface charge density increases. Researchers suggest that the repulsive effect may be an inherent property of electrically charged objects, a phenomenon that may have significant implications for the study of astrophysical jets and their behavior.
