The magnetic field structure of HD58260's active region, specifically the characteristics of its magnetic field, were studied using spectropolarimetry and a non-LTE model. A magnetic field configuration featuring a strong radial field was simulated, with a surface field strength of 2.5 kG and a magnetic field strength of 500 G at the boundary between the equator and poles. A radiative model was developed based on a hydrogen-rich stellar atmosphere, incorporating a two-level chromospheric model and a chromospheric discharge to account for the discrepancy between continuum and line formation heights. Several iron lines in the 3800-5000 Å range were computed under various equilibrium conditions, and their polarized signatures were analyzed. A comparison between theoretical calculations and observed measurements indicated a significant discrepancy between the surface and line formation height radial field strengths. Discharge effects were found to play a crucial role in altering the radial field's polarized signature, resulting in an observed polarized feature that was not present in the stationary radiative regime.

A new, simplified method for computing the Dunkl operator relevant to the saltmon polynomial in one dimension is introduced by connecting it to a free boson field, much like the approach used to define the SunInt package in the context of the Laplacian on the segment.

A recent study by the ALMA collaboration revealed the effectiveness of observing the 87 GHz (H30$\alpha$) line in tracing recent star formation within nearby galaxies. We have used ALMA data to map the H30$\alpha$ line in the z=0.032 galaxy NGC 5253 and compared it to other star-formation tracers. Our findings indicate that NGC 5253 exhibits H30$\alpha$ emission at a level comparable to its H$\alpha$ emission, even when accounting for the metallicity of the galaxy. A more in-depth examination of the emission revealed H30$\alpha$ emission originating from regions with higher stellar masses, a phenomenon attributed to the properties of the H30$\alpha$ line. We have successfully identified emission regions in NGC 5253 and discovered that the emission originates from the galaxy's disk, consistent with UV emission patterns. Our results demonstrate that the H30$\alpha$ line serves as a reliable indicator of recent star formation, particularly in metal-poor galaxies, and may be more effective than other tracers such as H$\alpha$ emission in certain contexts.

A topological dynamical system consists of a compact space and a measure-preserving transformation. It's considered ergodic if similar orbits under the group's action converge quickly, implying the group has an orbit. We found that continuous orbit similarity rigidity applies to minimally acting groups on compact groups with a finitely many orbits on the Chabauty-Fell topology group.

Estimating conditional expectation functions, where the dependent variable y is conditioned on explanatory variables x, poses a significant challenge due to data scarcity in high-dimensional x spaces. This problem is particularly pronounced when outcomes like mortality rates are predicted based on extensive data such as geographic and temporal locations. This study proposes a method to leverage information from similar data points and introduce a new nonparametric estimator for conditional expectation, the Local Constant Smoother (LCS). By utilizing an existing estimate of the conditional density, LCS provides a straightforward and effective solution, even in the presence of high-dimensional data. An extension of LCS, the Local Linear Smoker (LSL), is also presented to reduce bias, with a discussion on implementing these estimators in the presence of data dimensionality. LCS and LSL are shown to converge at optimal rates, matching the performance of nonparametric estimators in the one-dimensional case. Furthermore, the results of a Monte Carlo simulation demonstrate that LCS and LSL outperform traditional nonparametric estimators in terms of reduced variance. Empirical analysis of US-specific data demonstrates LCS's superiority in predicting mid-life mortality rates across varying locations.

We introduce an original evaluation framework focused on estimating the 
precise duration of epidemic processes. This research is driven by the need to 
establish suitable criteria for evaluating the quality of the estimator of 
duration. To address this, we define two novel criteria: (i) the 
asymptotic unbiasedness criterion and (ii) the mean squared duration estimator 
criterion. These are then utilized to assess various estimator types applied to 
different epidemic models. Notably, our theoretical analysis examines the 
performance of non-parametric kernel estimators and confirms their 
asymptotic unbiasedness while demonstrating their superior 
short-term bias-reducing capabilities over competing parametric estimators.

The integration of knowledge graphs (KGs) into information technology systems has led to significant advancements, however, they still have limitations due to existing information, resulting in incomplete KGs. Research has focused on linking future events in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs), which represent events in time-stamped data. Existing methods for forecasting future events use statistical or machine learning techniques, often for general knowledge graph completion. This study evaluates the effectiveness of three static framework-based approaches for the free linking of future events in TCGs. By incorporating temporal information through time distribution and time embedding, the proposed method achieves a higher recall rate compared to existing static framework-based approaches for future linking. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that static frameworks can be used for the effective forecasting of future events in TCGs.

Research focused on geometric properties of Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLKM) for advanced ultrafast lasers has been extensively pursued, yet it's crucial to acknowledge that these properties fluctuate during KLKM operation. This article investigates the impact of geometric variations on Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLKM) and establishes a new framework for understanding its complex nonlinear behavior. The concept of Transverse Nonlinearity Index (TNI) is introduced to evaluate geometric changes in a Kerr-lens mode-locked (KML) cavity, offering a means to analyze system stability. The TNI's change during the oscillation of an optical pulse provides insight into the onset of KLKM, while a decrease in TNI during pulse oscillation indicates system stability. The article also investigates the effect of nonlinear phase changes on the stability of Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLKM) and how it influences the system's nonlinear dynamics. The discussion is complemented by a case study of a specific KML oscillator and its behavior under varying conditions.

To train a machine learning model across multiple devices, such as a smartphone, without compromising user privacy, federated learning is utilized. This privacy-preserving approach allows for collaborative model development while keeping user data isolated. One of the most effective FL approaches is the asynchronous online federated optimization method, capable of training a model on large datasets efficiently. However, handling the device heterogeneity challenge poses significant issues, impacting both the training speed and model quality. To address this problem, we introduce a novel asynchronous online federated learning method that accounts for device heterogeneity. Our approach identifies a device's capabilities and training history, allowing it to adjust the number of data samples and machine learning model parameters for each device. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves the training speed and offers better model quality compared to existing FL approaches.

We've investigated the absorption properties of extremely thin silicon membranes in the near-infrared wavelength range, which are thin enough for the use of back-contact transistors. To enhance absorption, we've designed photonic crystal (PC) - patterned silicon membranes as well as those with an additional PC layer on the back, achieving a significant increase in absorption of over 90% at specific wavelengths. Using finite-difference time-domain simulations, we observed that these PC patterns can boost absorption up to 5 times in comparison to plain silicon membranes. Moreover, the PC patterns can rectify the properties of high-resistivity silicon by compensating for the impact of photonic absorption.

This paper demonstrates two key theorems regarding the asymptotic behavior of tetration: 
1. The recursive function $T_{k}(x)$, defined by $T_{k}(x) = x^{k\times T_{k}(x-1)}$ with $T_{k}(0) = 1$, can be approximated by its continuous version, tetration $^n_{k}x$, as $n$ approaches infinity. 
2. To calculate the constant term in this approximation, we require solving for another term, denoted by $\gamma_{k}$, which is defined by the equation $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\ln T_{k}(n)}{e^{n}} = \gamma_{k} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\ln ^{2}T_{k}(n)}{e^{n}} + \cdots$. 
To validate these theorems, we develop a general formula for analyzing the growth rate of iterated exponential functions, a critical component in understanding the asymptotic behavior of tetration.

High-dimensional expander (HDE) graphs to specific subspaces in $\mathbb{F}_2^d$ show promise in solving problems such as private information retrieval, distributed data storage, and network coding. We address the challenge of creating novel HDE graphs by proposing a systematic method based on covering one graph with another, which also yields general constructions and validates a different approach using products of smaller graphs.

Within the broader scope of exploring magnetic materials with the centered honeycomb lattice, our investigation focuses on GdInO$_3$, exhibiting a two-dimensional nature. By analyzing the magnetic susceptibility of GdInO$_3$ across a broad temperature range, our findings suggest that this substance is not a conventional Heisenberg antiferromagnet but rather a two-dimensional, layered ferromagnet that is coupled together by antiferromagnetic interactions. This is further confirmed by a comparison with existing theoretical models. Moreover, the presence of spin-phonon coupling in GdInO$_3$ is also observed.

The task of link forecasting in networks involves predicting whether a link will exist between two nodes $t$ time steps in the future, given the current network state and historical information. Graph autoencoders are commonly used in forecasting tasks, but their application to large-scale networks is hindered by high memory and computation requirements. To address this, we introduce a new feature embedding method that leverages the sparsity of network adjacency matrices to significantly reduce the size of similarity matrices. Experimental results on real-world networks demonstrate that this approach leads to more accurate link predictions and allows the use of graph autoencoders in large-scale networks, whereas previous methods were limited to smaller networks due to feasibility constraints.

To refine the frequency stability of optical lattice clocks, it's necessary to mitigate cold atom noise, which can be done by utilizing an enlarged surface area for efficient cooling and miniaturized optical pumping. A method to achieve this involves the use of micro-fabricated deep silicon vapor chambers, which can be integrated into a compact optical lattice setup. These chambers have a thin, micro-structured bottom and a thin top, separated by a small gap, and are ideal for integration within a silicon lattice clock due to their material and shape. A 100 mm cube optical lattice experiment successfully employed two micro-vapor chambers with 5 mm lateral dimensions and 5 mm depth for improved laser cooling and pump light absorption.

We investigated the impact of four-dimensional dual-polarization waveforms on the non-linear transmission impairments faced by single symbols in the time domain. To achieve this, we employed the time-domain Volterra series power balance equations to analyze four different dual-polarization waveforms in the presence of non-linear impairments. By considering the symmetry of these waveforms, we identified three distinct cases: (i) symmetry with equal power across the four waveforms, (ii) symmetry with varying power among the waveforms, and (iii) asymmetry with varying waveforms. To facilitate the analysis, we developed a vector-based model that is simpler to understand and comparable to the well-known effective SNR concept. This model enables us to quantify the four-fold power increase in the four-dimensional space and identify the power penalty associated with different waveforms. Furthermore, it helps us identify the optimal waveforms for specific system requirements.

Building upon the success of a recent deep learning-based visible-infrared fusion method, tailored for wildfire detection, a deep learning-based fusion network is developed to produce high-quality infrared images from low-quality infrared inputs and concurrent visible images. The proposed network, utilizing a deep convolutional neural architecture, incorporates an enhanced loss function and weakly-supervised learning to mimic the characteristics of the No-Object Region and Edge details preservation, along with introducing a new Mask Loss to handle low-quality infrared images' noise. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations on a self-curated LIDC dataset, highlighting its potential to significantly improve infrared image quality and the overall performance of the wildfire detection system.

Researchers have increasingly used social media data to gain insights into
diverse areas such as epidemiology and transportation, but few have provided
detailed data on how they accessed it. This research builds on previous work
conducting a data mining study to detect signs of depression through social media
posts. The associated data and code are available for public use. The study used
data from Twitter and Reddit, which were accessed via APIs and required
authentication. The search strategy involved specific hashtags and keywords related
to depression, which were then compared with randomly sampled posts. After
removing irrelevants, a human annotator classified the posts, resulting in 217
labeled posts. The performance of a machine learning model was evaluated using
these posts, as well as additional posts sampled from the same platforms,
revealing that targeted data collection significantly improved efficiency.

We divide the population into different groups based on their infection and recovery status, then apply a SIRS model to predict the dynamics within each section. Interactions between individuals occur based on a Poisson process. The movement of individuals between groups is modeled as a random walk system. The expected values of these system models form a system of ODEs, which we use to model the behavior of COVID-19 as a SIRS model. The model accounts for the fact that infected individuals may lose immunity and become susceptible again. The model equations are solved numerically using a non-deterministic finite difference method. The model's accuracy is evaluated by comparing the expected values of the infection and recovery state variables with data obtained during the COVID-19 pandemic in Iran. The results show a good match between the modeled expectations and the actual data.

Using the Shell Model, we investigate the ISGMR in 24Mg and 28Si, which are nuclei with low neutron excess, to understand the effects of coupling between ISGMR and quadrupole giant multipole (QGMR) intensity. Our results show that in 28Si, there is a notable contribution from QGMR to the ISGMR due to strong coupling, which is not the case in 24Mg. Additionally, we find that the E2/M1 transitions in 28Si are significantly stronger than in 24Mg, which is attributed to the stronger coupling in 28Si. Our calculations also reveal that the experimental ISGMR centroids in 24Mg and 28Si are underpredicted, which is due to the strong coupling with other states, particularly the isoscalar monopole quadrupole resonance (MGGMR) in 28Si. Our study suggests that the consideration of the coupling with the MGGMR is essential for accurate descriptions of ISGMR in 28Si.

A study of the dynamics of stable systems with Coulomb friction shows that feedback can cause oscillations and that these feedback-induced oscillations can be eliminated by choosing a damping parameter that is sufficiently large.

A new technique called Bellman Hedging, rooted in a game-theoretic understanding, has been developed to make deep reinforcement learning methods more stable and effective. This dynamic hedging strategy is designed to protect the main learner from the influence of poorly directed gradient updates by drawing inspiration from a related game called the Influence Game, where updates that support the value function are given priority. Our research shows that incorporating this idea into popular RL methods such as Actor-Critic, TRPO, and PPO significantly mitigates common learning instability issues and enhances the performance of these algorithms on complex control and Atari tasks. Notably, our modified versions of TRPO and PPO demonstrate substantial gains in sample efficiency and, upon closer inspection, reveal that hedging helps align the gradients of the value function, resulting in faster convergence.

To incorporate user motivation into sequential recommender systems, we suggest a Hidden Markov Model that captures underlying motivation states and their transitions. This model's parameters are automatically optimized through the EM algorithm using user interactions and item ratings. Our proposed method outperforms traditional sequential recommenders by considering both motivation states and user interactions, with the advantage of being easily adaptable to existing sequential recommenders and allowing for the incorporation of user interactions and item ratings.

It's been known for some time that a specific change can simplify the triconfluent Heun equation to its standard form, but this specific change was previously only valid when the equation had a particular type of symmetric potential with a source having a single peak. Our research now reveals that the change is actually part of a broader class of similar changes and confirms that it remains effective even when the source has multiple peaks. This knowledge allows us to map the general symmetric unfolded source potential onto the triconfluent Confluent Heun equation, providing a practical and versatile method for solving real-world problems in physics, such as those found in the threedim electron gas, by reducing the equation to the triconfluent form and then applying the known change to find a general solution.

We address a range of missing data recovery issues, including the problem of low rank matrix completion under the assumption that entries have a specific distribution. Specifically, it is assumed that a matrix can be decomposed into the outer product of two low-dimensional signals, each taking values from a limited set. To address scenarios in which these signals consist of groups with unique characteristics, we propose using a loss function derived from an entropy-based model that incorporates such group structures. To determine optimal recovery methods, we employ large-scale simulations to analyze the large-system limits of a group-structured model, revealing a distinct phase transition related to the rank of the underlying signals based on noise levels. To facilitate the analysis and optimization of our model's parameters, we develop an iterative algorithm for computing its essential limits, which converges under a specific condition. To validate our results, we apply them to reconstruct a simplified model of the human brain's connectivity, demonstrating improved performance when group structures are taken into account.

A fundamental principle underlies all symmetries, breaking through the nullity of the vacuum state to establish symmetry through the conserved Noether current. A unified vacuum model is proposed, incorporating the inherent lack of symmetry as a new concept. This innovative model eliminates the need for symmetries, rendering the Noether current and associated symmetries obsolete. The new vacuum model is defined by a singular current operator, J^S = 1. A novel topological model is derived from this operator, providing an alternative explanation for mass generation and particle creation that does not rely on symmetry breaking. Instead, this model attributes these phenomena to the inherent topological structure of the vacuum. The same principle applies to the weak interaction, where the inherent topological structure accounts for parity violation. The absence of weak symmetry in the vacuum does not necessitate spontaneous symmetry breaking. A comprehensive understanding of the universe's origin is provided by this unified vacuum model.

Semi-inclusive, forward-decay Lepton Flavor Equality (LFE) ratios in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions are proposed as robust observables that require minimal input from nonperturbative factors. These ratios, defined as comparisons between $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ and $b\to se^+$e decay rates, are found to be consistent with the predictions of the Standard Model (SM) at the 5% level. The LFE ratios offer an effective test for the validity of the LFE hypothesis in the context of new physics, particularly at the level of new physics effects that can be probed by the current muon g-2 anomaly. The LFE ratios' insensitivity to certain parameters and their relatively simple dependence on Wilson coefficients make them valuable tools in the search for new physics.

To achieve efficient interconnects between contemporary networks and legacy control systems, there's a growing need for flexible automation systems. This research presents a distributed approach to addressing reference tracking in linear multi-channel systems, allowing for the seamless integration of devices and systems with minimal recalibration. By implementing a data architecture that facilitates smooth communication, the proposed solution utilizes a distributed algorithm based on a consensus protocol, allowing for an unlimited number of controllers to be easily reconfigured and adapted to any system order, both stable and unstable, without needing to identify the overall system matrix or its related null spaces. This methodology offers the advantage of simple controller design through the use of proportional action and output tracking integral for each output channel.

The COVID19 pandemic has caused significant disruption worldwide, with the balance between social distancing and economic stability proving particularly challenging. To effectively manage the outbreak, the classification of COVID19 patients into two distinct categories is crucial: those who can be treated at home, and those requiring hospitalization. To address this, researchers have been exploring the use of AI-powered speech recognition systems, utilizing Python and the TensorFlow/keras BERT NLP model, to develop a voice-based application for COVID19 symptom assessment. This research proposes a two-stage classification model, initially designed to forecast the likelihood of a patient needing hospital care, and secondly, to provide an accurate diagnosis if the initial prediction is confirmed.

This article offers a comprehensive guide to essential open-source network analysis software, allowing researchers to seamlessly transition between different platforms based on their individual requirements. We provide annotated examples of widely used tools, including those available for Python (such as NetworkX, igraph, and the R packages {RNetSci} and {igraph}), as well as standalone applications for Gephi, YEd, and YAFI. Our analysis focuses on the capabilities of each tool for basic tasks like generating test networks, performing detailed network analysis, and visualizing results. We specifically highlight how each software handles specific network attributes and demonstrate its specific use cases.

The convergence between eco-evolutionary dynamics and eco-evolutionary time scales is a crucial factor in studying the evolution of growing populations. We propose a unified model that is adaptable to the evolution of populations with continuous or discrete generations, and that is applicable to various evolutionary rates. An eco-evolutionary damped oscillator is a common outcome of uniform evolutionary rates, while considering time scale modifiers can help to transition to resonant or anti-resonant eco-evolution dynamics, exemplified by limit cycles, spirals, and heteroclinic orbits. These dynamics can be further applied to a population that competes for resources, and the stability of eco-evolution dynamics can be assessed. We also explore a scenario where the evolutionary rate varies over time, which is observed in the evolution of bacteria under selection pressure in the lab, and find that this scenario can lead to anti-resonant dynamics, resulting in the persistence of maladaptive traits.

Current speech deep learning models are trained using large, publicly available datasets, which are often contaminated with malicious data. This study investigates the impact of hostile data on self-supervised speech learning, focusing on two types of attacks: label poisoning and data poisoning. Through controlled experiments, the research reveals that models trained on datasets contaminated with a small percentage of hostile data can experience significant performance decline. The findings also suggest that models trained on clean data are not immune to data poisoning attacks, even with a relatively low percentage of hostile data. The research's data poisoning attack dataset is publicly available for further study and validation of the findings.

Key advantages of decentralized technologies include the ability to operate without central control, eliminate single points of failure, and ensure the reliability of services. Despite decades of research, successful implementations of such technologies remain scarce. Embrace, a decentralized marketplace built on the Ethereum platform, showcases the benefits of these technologies. By leveraging existing Ethereum features like the blockchain, smart contracts, and various privacy measures, Embrace enables users to engage in anonymous transactions for goods and services. These features allow potential weaknesses to be transformed into strengths, providing a reliable and secure platform for users. In a comprehensive study, we examine the benefits of Embrace's architecture, conduct an in-depth analysis of its underlying components, and offer suggestions for improving the user experience.

A new method is developed to create sensitivity ranges in order to evaluate how reliable statistical results are in the face of incomplete data under specific conditions. This method is particularly useful in the context of observational studies where data collection issues frequently arise. In studies, effect estimates calculated from data can be influenced by both study design and statistical techniques used. This sensitivity analysis aids meta-analysts in understanding how much bias could be expected to exist in a study's outcome. This paper introduces a technique known as the E-value, which helps to determine the smallest amount of study bias that can account for an observed study effect, and then uses this information to create a corresponding E-confidence interval. This method is illustrated through its application to a study of the association between aspirin use and mortality among older individuals.

This study concludes the enumeration of all finite-dimensional symmetry factors for the quantum plane $Q[\mathbb{C}_\hbar^2]$. We demonstrate that each factor is a subalgebra of a specific representation of the De Concini-Kac-Vergne quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. By providing the corresponding symmetry factors for the quantum plane, we effectively provide a comprehensive list of finite-dimensional symmetry factors for the quantum plane. Our findings also reveal that $Q[\mathbb{C}_\hbar^2]$ and its subalgebra $\mathbb{C}_\hbar[x,y]^{\mathbb{Z}_2}$ exhibit distinct properties as they lack any finite symmetry factors. This study also revisits the classification of finite symmetry factors for the quantum affine plane $\mathbb{C}_\hbar[x,y;\partial_1,\partial_2]$.

The integration of federated learning and blockchain has gained traction in Internet of Vehicles (IoV) due to their capacity to address privacy and data security concerns. However, the development of FL-based blockchain frameworks in IoV is hindered by a lack of understanding of existing solutions and their respective advantages and disadvantages. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by providing a detailed review of blockchain-supported FL frameworks for IoV, categorized into three key aspects: consensus mechanisms, privacy preservation methods, and communication protocols. By examining a total of 54 relevant studies, this research identifies the most prominent features and methodologies employed in these frameworks. Furthermore, based on the literature analysis, this study highlights the respective benefits and drawbacks of each framework category, providing valuable insights for future FL and IoV developments.

The dynamics of bottom and charm production in hadron collisions can be studied by examining the ratios of beauty and charm yields, as they are directly linked to the gluon splitting fraction. A novel approach using prompt and non-prompt D mesons was employed to measure the beauty and charm production ratios at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV for the first time. For the first time, the production ratios were measured for D mesons with a high transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) in a collider environment. In addition, the production ratios of D mesons with varying $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ were calculated for the first time at the same high-energy proton-proton collisions. The results for the beauty and charm production ratios are in line with theoretical expectations from next-to-leading order perturbative quantum chromodynamics (NLO-PQCD) predictions. The ALICE collaboration's findings of the beauty and charm production ratios can be used to refine predictions for the future electron-ion collider (EIC).

The Department of Energy's SciQ Center at Fermilab's Main Campus has its physics laboratories maintained at a temperature significantly below room temperature, with certain areas even cooler, making an ideal setting for building a quantum computing platform. However, existing refrigeration equipment, such as dilution refrigerators, operates in a temperature range that is too warm for optimal quantum device performance. In contrast, Delft University of Technology has successfully created a custom-built dilution refrigerator with a final chamber temperature that is just 2.5 millikelvin above absolute zero. A joint effort between Fermilab and Delft is now underway to upgrade Fermilab's refrigeration equipment to this cooler temperature, with the aim of enabling quantum computing and sensor experiments at very low temperatures. Upgrading to this platform will benefit not only the SciQ project at Fermilab but also a wide range of experiments at its nearby laboratories.

Cryptographic primitives are essential security measures, yet improper implementation can result in severe security breaches. This essential knowledge is frequently absent from the educational backgrounds of many developers. To address this, our research aims to uncover and analyze real-world Python security vulnerabilities linked to the misuse of cryptographic tools. By combining static and dynamic analysis methods, we have examined a broad range of Python repositories, including open-source projects, security projects, and Python code present in binary applications. Our investigation has uncovered a surprising number of Python projects containing real-world exploits of cryptographic primitives, encompassing a wide variety of categories, project types, and sizes. Our research highlights the importance of ensuring proper education on cryptographic implementation for developers and emphasizes the necessity for comprehensive static analysis tools capable of detecting such misuses.

This paper presents a novel automated evaluation method, called Virtual Automatic Labeling Engine, to enhance the reliability of user annotations in UMSO datasets, resolving the issue of inconsistent or unreliable user tags. By employing a scale voting mechanism, the server assesses and optimizes tag quality, eliminating low-quality annotations and promoting high-quality ones. A virtual agent simulates human evaluation to gather and process opinions, then the annotations are revised based on the scale. To further validate the technique's effectiveness, the project tests it on Amazon Mechanical Turk by comparing original and revised annotations. The results show significant improvements in tag quality and provide support for the technique's efficacy.

This study proposes a sparse reconstruction approach for seismic reflectivity, drawing inspiration from the Successive Proximal Mean (SPM) algorithm. While SPM has been effective for image reconstruction, it suffers from a limitation of uniform sampling. A new network architecture, the Proximal Mean Network (NuSPAN), is introduced to address this issue by using nonuniform, sparse sampling. The NuSPAN network is capable of approximating the proximal mean operator, and its parameters can be learned using backpropagation. Additionally, the NuSPAN network is combined with the Landweber iteration (LW) algorithm to develop a deep learning-based inverse solver for seismic reflectivity reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the NuSPAN network over its uniformly sampled counterpart and the traditional LW algorithm.

This investigation focuses on the semigroups of composition operators, specifically within spaces that mirror the properties of BMOA, a space of functions analytic on the unit disk with bounded mean oscillation. These properties are examined in relation to an integral-based criterion, which determines whether a semigroup falls into the category of extended BMOA, a notion known as the extended BMOA-type spaces.

The study of two-dimensional systems with topological order is a significant area of research, but it remains limited by the lack of solvable examples beyond the toric code. Recent discoveries have revealed additional topological models, but they are not exactly solvable and require numerical analysis. To gain insights into these models, it is essential to study the finite-size corrections of their physical properties. A new, general method has been developed to determine critical exponents and universal finite-size corrections for topological models by analyzing wavefunction overlaps of corresponding conformal field theories, specifically the Haagerup model. This method was previously not feasible due to the unknown critical data, but is now applicable thanks to the identification of the relevant conformal field theory.

To facilitate accurate language processing, historical texts require Part-of-Speech (POS) analysis, which is complicated by historical language variations. We tackle this complexity by applying a set-valued prediction approach, allowing for the representation of historical words' ambiguous POS. Utilizing the projected stochastic gradient method and encoding POS labels as geometric shapes in a latent space, our method produces accurate results. Notably, experimentally, our approach outperformed previous methods by 4.5% in POS labeling accuracy for 18th-century German.

This paper delves into the non-uniform integrability of measurable functions. The focus lies on vacuuming families of sets, which play a crucial role in characterizing non-uniform integrability. A key outcome is the derivation of a KRT-type criterion specifically for non-uniform integrability. Additionally, we establish a characterization of a k-summable vacuuming family in terms of a specific countable set within the background sigma-algebra. Another result shows that the union of a countable collection of vacuuming families maintains its vacuuming property, provided it is k-summable, and even provides a KRT-type criterion for this vacuuming family. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between non-uniform integrability and a specific type of counting measure defined on sigma-algebras.

We introduce a cutting-edge system that streamlines converting urban requirements into formal specifications, utilizing both deterministic and non-deterministic state machine representations. This system is grounded in the UrSAFL language, a novel formalism for describing urban state machines, enabling versatile modeling without being constrained to specific models. We've developed AFLUR, an open-source tool for parsing UrSAFL files, and integrated it with Ambrosia, a dynamic code evaluation platform, to facilitate the automatic generation of both public and private code, ensuring requirements compliance. This code is tailored for deployment within city environments, with options for open-source, proprietary integration, or deployment on decentralized city blockchains to guarantee unalterable requirements.

This paper introduces a novel quantum error correction technique for stabilizing complex quantum computing systems, building upon the reliable methods of classical computing. It adapts a previously successful quantum protocol to effectively address faults in superconducting processing units. It utilizes well-established, high-fidelity gates and measurements to locate and correct errors. Conventional error correction methods often necessitate a precise understanding of the error's origin and implement corrective operations at that point. In contrast, this protocol's concealing properties allow it to pinpoint an error without identifying its source and execute error correction operations elsewhere, thereby minimizing additional errors and improving success rates. Demonstration experiments are carried out with real-world superconducting processing equipment to validate the protocol's efficacy.

Equivalence relations in a regular category are defined as subobjects that are projections of biproducts. The term "cocartesian" is used to describe such equivalence relations where the projections form universal arrows for the canonical maps projecting biproducts. These projections are typically continuous, meaning they preserve limit-related maps. This article demonstrates that in any regular category, there exists an equivalence between equivalence relations that are cocartesian and subobjects that are both retracts and closed under the category's regular structure.

A statistical model has been created to analyze and predict extreme weather conditions in specific geographic areas, using data from the energy sector's offshore operations. This model was put to the test by examining the North Sea, and we analyzed the likelihood of simultaneous extreme weather events occurring at two different locations, as well as the impact of one location's conditions on the other. Using extreme value theory, we investigated the relationship between the conditions at the two locations, and found that they tend to move in the same direction, becoming more correlated as the weather conditions become increasingly extreme. Additionally, we used a statistical tool called spatial extreme value conditional quantile simulation to estimate the probability of extreme weather conditions occurring in the North Sea, given a certain threshold. Our analysis also revealed how extreme weather conditions at the Grimsby energy transition test site could impact the Muckle Flugga oil platform in the Shetland Islands, and how this impact changes depending on the severity of the weather.

State-of-the-art vision-language models like VT-CLIP excel at zero-shot tasks, including image-text classification and retrieval, by leveraging large-scale training data. These models' semantic understanding capabilities are primarily driven by a strong text encoder and a visually informative image encoder. To further enhance the image feature representation in these models, a text-based bootstrapping approach is introduced. Specifically, VT-CLIP incorporates a multi-modal attention module that leverages auxiliary image patches to refine text embeddings and guide the learning of more discriminative visual features. By adding auxiliary pixel patch inputs, the proposed approach can capture finer-grained visual patterns and produce discriminative multi-modal features. Experiments demonstrate the efficacy of VT-CLIP on a range of benchmark datasets, including the standard COCO-REtrieval and image captioning tasks, and various image classification benchmarks. Notably, the proposed approach achieves a substantial 3.6% improvement in VT-CLIP's mAP score on the PASCAL-REtrieval dataset.

We suggest using operator transitioning to mitigate the effects of operator noise in a general setting. This method has been applied successfully in a operator scaling context and can be used to develop a quantum algorithm for solving linear systems. The proposed noisiness framework can be adapted to other operators and even non-linear operators.

Our main finding is that for $k \geqslant 2$, $\pi_{n}\bigl(\Seg E_{\ff}(H\ff[{\fp}],\ff)\bigr) \cong \pi_{n}\bigl(\Seg E_{\ff}(H\ff[{\fp}^{\ff^{-1}}],\ff)\bigr) \cong \pi_{n-1}\bigl(\Sigma_{\fp} H\ff[{\fp}^{-1}]\ff\bigr)$ for all primes $\fp$ dividing $p$ and all $n$, where $\pi_{n-1}\bigl(\Sigma_{\fp} H\ff[{\fp}^{\ff^{-1}}]\ff\bigr) \cong \pi_{n-1}\bigl(\Sigma_{\fp} H\ff[{\fp}^{-1}]\ff\bigr) \cong 0$ for the prime $\fp=p$ and $\pi_{n-1}\bigl(\

Given an m-dimensional local ring R with a residue field that is perfect and nilpotent-invariant, we define the tight Hilbert function f and polynomial f for R. We find that if r is a sufficiently large non-negative integer, then the tight Hilbert function becomes a polynomial of degree 2m. In the one-dimensional case, we demonstrate that for any non-zero ideal I in R, the tight Hilbert function f equals a newly defined polynomial p*(I) of degree one, consisting of non-negative coefficients. We also establish that for any system of parameters x in R, the tight Hilength l^*(x) equals the length of the quotient R over the I-adic completion of R times x, for a specific ideal I. This leads to the conclusion that for any system of parameters x in R, the tight Hilbert function f equals a linear combination of length of quotients R over parameter-generated ideals, each with a unique set of parameters.

Machine learning models are increasingly being used in medical image analysis, with potential for improving diagnostic accuracy and workflow efficiency. However, the integration of these models into clinical workflow is hindered by a lack of standardized reporting methods for model performance and accuracy. The reporting standards, such as RADIODIKOM and PATHIODIKOM, have been developed to address this issue, but a practical implementation is still needed. A new Python framework, called Highdicom, is proposed to facilitate the creation of reports that comply with these standards. The framework provides functionality for generating machine learning model outputs and integrating them with existing medical imaging data, such as DICOM images. The proposed framework is demonstrated using examples from both pathology and radiology, highlighting its versatility and potential applications.

We investigate the implications of the conformal anomaly on the Virasoro algebra in 2D spacetime with a dynamic boundary, revealing that the cosmological constant and a specific coefficient of the Ricci scalar at the boundary contribute to the central charge. The coefficient of the Ricci scalar within the gravitational action can be set freely, yet its associated coefficient in the counterterm, when used to regularize the action, is determined by the variation of the central charge. We then examine the effect of a change in the associated coefficient on the central charge in spacetime with a dynamic boundary, and in turn, how this affects the conformal anomaly in 2D. Furthermore, we study the impact of introducing disorder into the gravitational action, specifically in the form of a step-function-like perturbation to the Lagrangian density, and how this influences the Virasoro algebra, specifically its zero mode.

In the case of a sequence-based object, our approach involves breaking down the sequence into fixed-sized segments that serve as the basis for further analysis. These segments are then used as input to a deep neural network that learns distinct patterns of features. Unlike other methods that rely on pre-defined features, our unattended model allows the neural network to determine effective features directly from the sequence. Once the segments and network are established, they can be applied to classify a sequence into classes or to determine the location of specific regions within a sequence. Notably, our method is computationally efficient, as it can process a sequence of length $N$ in $O(N)$ time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the learned patterns of features can be visualized using established techniques, revealing particularly significant characteristics. A proof-of-concept application of our approach is presented in the context of identifying DNA binding sites for transcription factors.

The transition between metallic and insulating states in various materials can be induced by manipulating external factors such as pressure, temperature, and doping levels. Nonetheless, this metal-insulator shift is not fully understood in many cases and can even be reversed with changes in the sample's surface termination. In order to gain a deeper understanding of this phenomenon, researchers have employed a computational method called density functional theory to study the electronic structure of very thin, single-layered films of V$_2$O$_3$ with different surface terminations. Through this study, it was discovered that the metal-insulator shift in V$_2$O$_3$(0001) ultrathin films is dependent on termination and that an insulating phase can be achieved in an ultrathin film with 7 layers, whereas the bulk form of V$_2$O$_3$ undergoes a metal-insulator transition at high temperatures. Researchers have proposed that the metal-insulator shift in these ultrathin films is due to changes in orbital occupancy and surface charge, and have found that these changes are consistent with findings from research on other materials, such as VO$_2$ and CrO$_2$.

This paper explores the Clebsch authorization of a Lie-Poisson Hamiltonian system, leveraging Lie-Poisson coordinates along with Clebsch variables. A particular focus is placed on a Hamiltonian reflecting a system's kinetic energy and a external potential, with subsequent examination of a specific instance - the Euler equations for inviscid flow.

A series of six articles have been published, detailing the results of a systematic analysis of irregular planetary orbits using data from the South African Astronomical Observatory. This paper presents the findings from a thorough review of a complete sample of 23 exoplanets from the KMTNet-APIS project, which was based on irregular light curves. After accounting for factors such as ellipsoidal distortion, reflection, and the presence of rings, a total of 11 planets were found to have no statistically significant ring models, while 12 planets with periods under 40 days were found to have rings. For a subset of these planets, a significant inclination is detected, and ring opening ratios are estimated. Furthermore, the phase function and precession of ring nodes are predicted for nodes that are not edge-on, and the mass of a planet with a ring is estimated. The findings suggest that a significant portion of all known exoplanets may possess ring systems, and that this trend is more pronounced for planets with longer orbital periods.

We have developed a novel method for incorporating the principles of conservation directly into numerical models, using a scheme based on compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Unlike previous approaches, this scheme does not utilize re-construction of conserved quantities, employing instead a unique combination of finite volume and finite element techniques. A key component of this method involves the utilization of a specific flux calculator, which facilitates accurate numerical calculations. Moreover, to maintain numerical stability, a volume-preserving, Lagrange multiplier-based isoparametric finite element has been introduced, coupled with a finite volume Navier-Stokes solver. The effectiveness of this scheme has been demonstrated through a series of test cases. Additionally, a comprehensive description of this scheme has been provided in an accompanying paper.

Determining whether a molecule is superconducting poses a significant challenge for the physics community, as it's essential for the development of the Next-Generation LHC. Leveraging machine learning, researchers have successfully achieved high accuracy in predicting superconducting characteristics, thanks to advanced algorithms utilizing extensive data sets. Our study compares the performance of various machine learning methods, including Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting, in classifying superconducting characteristics on a modified, larger proton number learning dataset. Our analysis also investigates the importance of specific features in the machine learning models and their impact on classification results.

We introduce a new method of calculating the chromatic symmetric functions for certain Dyck path graphs, which we expand to be similar to the q-rook theory. This method leads to the development of a conjecture for the chromatic symmetric functions of Young diagrams.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks have achieved top-notch results on image classification tasks due to their ability to learn translation-invariant features. However, this translation-invarity also causes them to ignore the direction of objects within an image, which can be crucial for classification. In response, we introduce a new type of convolution known as orientation convolution, and based on this, we develop the Orientation Convolutional Network (OCON), which is sensitive to the orientation of objects within an image. Experimental results on the Cifar10 dataset show that networks incorporating a significant proportion of orientation convolutions perform better than their counterparts using traditional convolutions, and OCON can effectively identify the direction of handwritten digits on this dataset.

Given two finite real unipotent groups U and V along with finite relative invariant measures μU and μV, we can construct a new relative invariant measure on the semidirect product U×*V based on μU and μV. Our formula links the triple relative invariant measures to integrals of invariant relative traces and a novel relative trace invariant of the triple.

A substantial, flavor-specific top quark mass anomaly is discovered through the exploration of a novel top quark observable, specifically its twist-2 flavor-dependent mass $m_t^{q\bar{q}}$. By employing the strategy of matching parton distribution functions (PDFs) with parton-to-parton cross sections, a flavor-specific top quark mass mass fraction is derived for this observable, revealing that it is composed largely of a photon-top loop diagram. As a result, determination of $m_t^{q\bar{q}}$ from a future electron-proton collider, such as the European Nuclear Collider (ENC), will yield an effective top quark mass $m_t^{\rm EFEL}$, dominated by $m_t^{q\bar{q}}$ and a photon-top loop diagram. This implies that $m_t^{\rm EFEL}$ will exhibit a substantial, and flavor-dependent top quark mass shift relative to the standard hadronic mass $m_t^{\rm SPAL}$. This top quark mass shift is found to be on the scale of a GeV, significantly surpassing the hadronic mass uncertainty of a few hundred MeV. This phenomenon is attributed to the substantial nature of $m_t^{q\bar{q}}$ and its W-fusion and Z-boson exchange contributions. We demonstrate a hypercontractive inequality for the weighted Bergman spaces in the unit disk, where the weight depends on an even integer power of the modulus.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused a significant global health crisis, with numerous fatalities and widespread infections. To address the challenge of diagnosing infected individuals, which typically involves contact with healthcare professionals and risks of viral transmission, researchers have investigated the use of artificial intelligence for pulmonary evaluation. To achieve accurate AI-based diagnosis, high-quality, over-sampled data is required, which is often not available in many countries. To address this limitation, we propose a COVID-19 detection approach that can perform well even with limited data, by employing a dataset with a diverse range of low-dose chest CT images, including those with normal and abnormal characteristics, collected from multiple hospitals in the United States. To address the class imbalance issue inherent in such datasets, we developed a two-stage time-distributed capsule network. To mitigate the effects of over-regularization, the first stage involves a time-distributed capsule network, while the second stage incorporates a capsule fusion module. To address the challenge of class imbalance, we further proposed a method to adjust the capsule fusion scores, which resulted in improved diagnostic accuracy.

This study focuses on organizing space resources in the Low Earth Orbits. Theoretical research is conducted to develop an organized structure for utilizing Low Earth Orbits in a coordinated and organized manner. The goal is to categorize and utilize a specific class of satellites - Intersatellites - that operate at an altitude of approximately 1,000 km. The study utilizes the principles of Celestial Mechanics to establish an ordered set of satellite orbits based on their orbital elements. The resulting structure, known as the 'Cosmic Order', consists of interlinked layers, each representing a group of satellites on adjacent orbital planes, which can be visualized as a three-dimensional honeycomb structure. The study focuses on modeling the communication capabilities within the Cosmic Order and determining the number of Intersatellites required to maximize communication range. The findings indicate that the maximum communication range is achieved when the number of satellites on each orbital plane is 18. The study also examines the communication range for different values of signal transmission rate.

Creating high-quality tetrahedral meshes from Computer Aided Design (CAD) models poses significant challenges, particularly in accurately capturing key features such as corners, curves, and surfaces. To address this issue, we introduce a novel method for generating high-order quad-based meshes on the 2D boundary of such models. By employing a combination of linear programming techniques and careful selection of parameters, our approach ensures the creation of dense, uniform quadrilateral grids. The resulting mesh can then serve as a starting point for subsequent 3D tetrahedral volume meshing processes, ultimately leading to improved overall mesh quality.

The multivariate normal distribution of sample correlation values is well-established in statistical literature. However, when considering uniform distributions over the interval of possible correlation values, from negative one to positive one, there is less understanding. Our research delves into correlator permutons, a concept that examines possible arrangements of data points in terms of correlation values, and is a part of permutationon research. We derive analytical formulas that provide key insights into the statistical characteristics of these objects, specifically their average moments and variability. These findings are particularly significant for understanding the statistical behavior of corramutons under various distribution models, with a current focus placed on the multivariate normal and uniform distributions.

The principle of general relativity's S-matrix provides a clear framework for constructing the Einstein equations. By applying a similar approach to higher-spin fields, we derive a unique set of equations. Notably, this method also allows us to construct novel interactions for spin-2 and spin-3 matter fields, providing a path to extending beyond Einstein's theory of gravity. Specifically, we demonstrate the recovery of $\alpha$-attractor models when the spin of the matter field is $s=2$.

This research aims to address the control issue in the $d$-dimensional ($d\geq 2$) incompressible $L^q$ Navier-Stokes equations system. By applying a finite dimensional interior feedback control, we establish in this paper that the controlled system possesses a unique globally attracting universal bounded weak solution. Our approach demonstrates that this absorbing weak solution is further proven to be the unique globally attracting universal strong solution, provided $q$ meets specific conditions, specifically $q\geq 3$ or $q=2$. Ultimately, our work shows that the controlled system can be viewed as a d-dimensional $2\lambda$-Laplace fluid with $0<\lambda<1/4$.

LitMind's lexicography software, listed on GitHub, provides a dictionary functionality through a web interface. The development of LitMind's dictionary leverages pre-existing resources, making it a collaborative tool that can be enhanced by adding entries in various formats, including JSON-LD, XML, XSLT, XSL, XSLXSL, XSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSL, XSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLXSLX

Recent research has exposed several issues with LIME's ability to generate accurate interpretations for neural networks, specifically in the context of recommender systems. A modified version of LIME, called LIME-RS, was introduced to address these limitations. To enhance the reliability of LIME-RS, we propose an optimization technique that increases model consistency, and evaluate its effectiveness in comparison to other methods through simulations. By treating LIME-RS explanations as virtual side information, we also introduce a dynamic regularization method to refine the underlying models, resulting in improved performance and more reliable explanations. Our findings indicate that our approach outperforms other methods, and LIME-RS can be effectively leveraged as a regularization tool to enhance the model's predictive accuracy.

On a semi-insulating silicon substrate, this structure consists of a thin quantum well and two highly doped cap layers.  By varying the well thickness, the carriers in the doped cap layers contribute to a two-dimensional density of states within the near-surface structure, whose energy levels can be precisely measured using photoluminescence.  The resulting fermi level anchoring within the dark exciton state is then investigated.  The results show that the fermi level is fixed at the dark exciton state for structures with energy levels above the fermi level. In the context of non-iid data, regional query sampling is a widely used technique for improving the robustness of machine learning models, especially in federated learning settings. Regional query sampling involves training a model on local subregions of each client's data, which helps mitigate the adverse effects of outliers and improves the overall model's performance. However, the effectiveness of regional query sampling depends on the shape and distribution of each client's data, and it may not always outperform global query sampling. To address this, this study investigates under what conditions regional query sampling can outperform global query sampling, and it reveals that the round-robin global query method can be more effective in certain scenarios. Furthermore, the research shows that both regional and round-robanin query methods can suffer from a phenomenon called "data shape bias," which may cause the model to focus on specific data shapes. Finally, the study presents a new algorithm called Local-Global Query, which uses a combination of global and local query methods to address the data shape bias issue and improve the model's robustness.

The performance of deep learning models is often hindered by their inability to address dataset imbalance, a problem that's been effectively tackled by Optimal Transport (OT). Although previous attempts to implement OT have yielded models with improved performance, they were limited by their computational constraints. Building upon our earlier work introducing Quick Sinkhorn, an algorithm that enables efficient OT computation, we introduce a novel approach - an iterative triangular matrix-based formulation of OT that can be calculated in linear time. This approach, when combined with data augmentation, has successfully enabled the accurate segmentation of a highly challenging dataset - lung CT scans - in just a fraction of the time required by existing methods.

The young star AU Mic, known for its variability, is studied in the context of its relationship with planets AU Mic b and c. This study examines the star's behavior during quiescent periods and eruptions, particularly focusing on the connection between stellar activity and the planets. Observations of AU Mic's quiescent periods indicate that the star's activity is not significantly higher than other stars in a similar magnitude range. During eruptions, the star's behavior is characterized by a combination of chromospheric emission and white light flares. Analysis of these flares reveals a ratio of X-ray to optical energy that is lower than expected. The occurrence of high-ionization lines and the absence of significant variability in the star's FUV emission suggest that the star's activity is not primarily driven by coronal activity. Instead, variability in the star's FUV and optical emissions indicates activity concentrated in the star's chromosphere. Furthermore, during periods of high-energy flares, the star's FUV variability is observed to increase. These findings have significant implications for the connection between the star's activity and the atmospheric evolution of AU Mic c.

The concept of drag force is revisited, focusing on the response of a substance medium. Two key points are emphasized: Firstly, the response current is the primary factor, while radiation fields are secondary; the response current generates the emitted radiation. Secondly, the velocity of a charged particle does not solely dictate the radiation response, as it is influenced by the medium's spatial nonlocality, modeled as a fluid with momentum. This momentum fluid exhibits nonlocal characteristics, with the particle's velocity having a transverse component that contributes to the emitted radiation, resulting in a radiation reaction loop, where the charged particle's motion is influenced by the emitted radiation field, further modifying the response current.

Real-world data often contains irregularities in terms of class distribution, a phenomenon referred to as data unevenness. Traditional closest neighbor classification methods are not well-suited for addressing this issue. In this paper, a novel statistical approach is proposed to enhance the performance of closest neighbor classification on uneven data. This method assigns varying weights to neighbors based on their class probabilities. The validity of this approach is proven by demonstrating that the proposed classifier converges to a closest neighbor classifier as the sample size increases. Through simulation studies and real-world applications, the efficacy of this approach is demonstrated to surpass that of traditional closest neighbor classification methods.

We have identified 1,034 quasars ranging from $z$ = 1.5 to 3.5 with a magnitude of $g$ $\le$ 17.5 using the SkyMapper survey, and combined this with previously published catalogs to create a comprehensive, uniform luminosity function for the specified redshift range. Our results show that the luminosity function for $z$ $\ge$ 3.5 is better constrained than previously, and that it peaks around $M_{\rm{AGN}}$ = -27.5. Furthermore, we observed that the luminosity function for $z$ $\ge$ 3.5 is flatter than that for $z$ < 3.5, and that there is a discrepancy between the luminosity functions for $M_{\rm{AGN}}$ < -27.5 and those above. This is likely due to the incompleteness of our sample for both very luminous quasars and those at lower redshifts.

Exploring quantum dot and superconducting combinations through charge sensing reveals a significant potential for studying unconventional superconductivity. However, the relationship between these systems is complex, involving multiple tunneling mechanisms that can be influenced by quantum dot positioning. By positioning a quantum dot relatively far from the superconducting electrode, we demonstrate that a distinct superconducting resonance emerges, which is not observed in the usual Coulomb blockade spectrum, but rather in gate spectroscopy. Furthermore, we find that this phenomenon indicates a two-component order parameter, which may be spatially modulated, as suggested by the presence of a resonance corresponding to the dot's lowest energy level. These findings indicate that when positioned appropriately, quantum dot measurements can provide valuable insights into the underlying superconducting mechanisms.

Contractive laws are a subset of hyperbolic conservation laws, characterized by a metric that remains invariant under the solution path. By incorporating a Lipschitz-continuous Lie point condition, contractions gain a contractivity flux that enables the identification of weak entropic discontinuities, which satisfy the entropic inequality at non-entropy solutions. This concept is applied to a framework of anisotropic conservation laws, which encompass both isentropic shocks and Riemann invariants as special cases, extending a prior study by Bressan, Goatin, and Khanmamedov. The contractivity is driven by a Lyapunov-type measure, which is adapted to a general Riemann invariant, its corresponding entropy variables, and a suitable entropy measure, all of which satisfy a compatibility condition. The resulting weak discontinuities are characterized by their entropic inequality, a shock admissibility condition, and an entropy inequality, which can be expressed in terms of a suitable entropy and a shock speed that satisfies a specific condition.

We envision a dreamlike experience for users, where they can explore imaginative worlds created by their own mental imagery. To achieve this, we've developed a reliable system for generating continuous, interactive 3D environments based on a single image and user instructions. Our system combines 360-degree scene reconstruction from single images with text-conditioned view extensions to create seamless, navigable worlds. To enhance efficiency, our method utilizes pre-trained diffusion models, allowing it to produce high-quality 360-degree images without the need for related image pairs or 3D models. Through our approach, users can step into fantastical dream worlds, where they can interact with their imagination in real-time.

The highly interconnected nature of modern networks greatly amplifies the potential risks posed by disturbances and cyber threats to critical infrastructure, such as power grids and transportation systems. Notably, the spread of cyber malware on these networks can be likened to the transmission of infectious diseases, where vulnerable nodes become infected, thereby increasing the likelihood of neighboring nodes to also contract the malware. To effectively manage such complex and control problems, researchers have proposed using techniques from data-driven science. This study investigates a stochastic network model, known as the networked SIS epidemic model, which simulates the spread of an infectious disease on a network. By analyzing this model, we demonstrate how data-driven science can predict and enhance the behavior of complex systems, including networks, without relying on precise system models or even the underlying equations of stochastic processes. Our findings show that data-driven science is a promising approach for managing complex systems, including networks, in an era where information is abundant but understanding is limited.

An experiment was conducted to study the behavior of a pool of liquid on a fiber under specific conditions where the surface tension exceeds gravity. The pool undergoes an instability, breaking into equally spaced droplets, and the process is observed to proceed in two stages. Initially, the break-up occurs in an unstable manner with a frequency that is influenced by the thickness of the liquid and its surface tension. As the instability progresses, the formation of droplets is seen to be on a scale larger than the thickness of the liquid. In the second stage, the break-up process is reduced by a factor of two, and the formation of droplets is seen to be on a scale similar to the thickness of the liquid. The observed behavior aligns with theoretical predictions regarding the effect of surface viscosity and surface tension on the break-up process.

Assessing scoliosis using ultrasound is an effective approach for detecting the condition early, particularly in children and infants. However, the process of manually scanning these patients is often difficult and time-consuming. In this study, a robotic ultrasound system was tested for its ability to assess scoliosis in 15 infants and children under the age of 5, in comparison to a traditional manual method. The accuracy of the robotic system was evaluated based on its ability to identify the anatomical landmarks and curvature angles accurately. The results showed that the robotic system had a high degree of reliability in both identifying anatomical landmarks and measuring curvature angles, with an average error of 0.9 degrees and 1.1 degrees, respectively. Furthermore, the reliability of the robotic system was demonstrated through repeated measurements, with an average error of 0.8 degrees and 0.6 degrees, respectively. The findings of this study suggest that the use of robotics can improve the reliability of ultrasound imaging for scoliosis evaluation.

In the field of speech and text research, the synthesis of speech samples with realistic durations is crucial for effective sentence length matching. A new, non-statistical method has been developed to calculate the expected speech duration for specific spoken words by utilizing a sentence-based, bottom-up, non-statistical approach. This method, uniquely suited to the task, differs from the typical top-down, sentence-independent, statistical models. A key component of this approach involves using the median of spoken durations from all available samples, which is then used to adjust the rate of speech in a synthesis engine to match the target duration for each text unit.

The growing prevalence of online hate speech poses a significant challenge to online communities. As a result, a substantial number of moderators manually review hate speech, placing high demands on communities to reduce moderation costs. Characterizing hate speech characteristics is a crucial first step in developing effective hate speech detection systems. In this study, a novel feature extraction technique is introduced to automatically identify distinct types of online hate speech characteristics, including semantic, syntactic, and online context features. Moreover, this research demonstrates the efficacy of deep learning models in extracting features and a character-level Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) auto-encoder in capturing the sequential nature of online communication. Through experimental evaluation, our proposed approach is demonstrated to be effective, robust, and capable of generalizing well across communities.

This research introduces a two-tier, collaborative MIMO structure, where the first base station shares its key signal characteristics with the secondary MIMO base station. To optimize this sharing process, the authors suggest the use of an autoencoder technique within the inter-BS connection. This allows the secondary BSS to reconstruct the primary BSS's features accurately, while also enabling efficient transmission over the inter-BS channel. A key advantage of the proposed approach lies in its ability to maintain a significant gain in spectral efficiency, even when the inter-BS channel is constrained. This is exemplified in the digital beamforming application, where the authors demonstrate how the proposed structure can be effectively implemented. Furthermore, the researchers examine the impact of the primary BSS's key characteristics on the overall system efficiency.

Historical archives contain invaluable knowledge encapsulated within records and images, which hold profound significance for research. Unfortunately, these documents are often compromised by deterioration, rendering them unreadable and limiting their accessibility for further analysis. The rapid advancement of digital technologies has propelled the development of digital restoration techniques, which have been accelerated by an increased availability of historical record image datasets. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of historical record image datasets available in online platforms, encompassing images from East Asian, European, and South American sources, aiming to fill a knowledge gap by providing an in-depth, scholarly analysis of existing datasets.

We introduce a smoothness-based control method for industrial robots to optimize
particular tasks, like package delivery, to make them more human-centric. Our
auxiliary feedback signal is generated using task speed and acceleration data to
fine-tune the robot's behavior. This signal is simple in concept and easy to
implement on existing robots. We also develop a model for predicting end-effector
forces to ensure safety and create a closed-loop system that balances this force
model with the smoothness-based control to maintain desired force levels. Our
results in evaluating the method on a KUKA KR500 robot demonstrate its potential to
improve task smoothness by factors of 2 to 5 compared to standard programming.

A statistical framework is developed to analyze recurrent health issues, such as heart attacks, that can be viewed as events occurring over a person's lifetime. This research introduces a novel method to assess not only the frequency of these events but also the accompanying transitions in a person's health state. By applying a joint model, the study investigates how initial health characteristics, specifically for patients who have already experienced a heart attack, influence their future heart health. By considering the interconnectedness of a person's health over time, the proposed methodology provides a more comprehensive understanding of their life trajectory.

The concept of molecular continuum is a widely used approximation to model protein solvation and binding processes, allowing for more efficient calculations than all-atom solvation models. A major challenge lies in accurately accounting for the van der Waals surface's irregularities when calculating the molecular continuum potential. To address this, existing methods utilize a combination of a grid-based approach near the surface and a point-based approach further away. However, the transition between these two regions poses a numerical challenge. In this research, we develop a new method that employs a grid-based approach throughout the space but divides it into multiple sites to enhance accuracy and efficiency. By using different grid resolutions for different sites, we achieve an accurate representation of the molecular surface while maintaining computational speed. To validate our method, we apply it to a multi-site Poisson-Boltzmann model and evaluate its accuracy and efficiency through numerical tests. Furthermore, we apply this method to a molecular dynamics simulation to analyze the solvation entropy of a peptide, demonstrating the method's effectiveness and efficiency.

We investigate the complexity of the metric dimension problem, focusing on specific parameterizations and modifications. When restricted to chordal graphs, the metric dimension problem is NP-hard, even when a vertex cover of size k is provided. This result extends to graphs with k feedback vertex groups, and also applies to parameterizations by clique cover or partial feedback vertex group. Consequently, we obtain an f(k)-2^{k^2} algorithm for the metric dimension problem, and further, an approximation hardness result in combination with the vertex cover problem.

A new type of hierarchical structure, called an authority framework, is defined.
Authority frameworks can be seen as a type of hypergraph and can be represented as an authority framework if and only if they can be embedded in the framework of the lexicographic product of two smaller hypergraphs.
This framework is self-similar in the sense of fractals and its set-theoretic complexity is proven.
An authority framework is equivalent to a set of points in n-dimensional space that can be mapped onto each other while preserving the framework's structure, and this equivalence is shown to be undecidable.
A new type of hypergraph called a shadow framework is defined, which is characterized by a simple condition.
Shadow frameworks are used to approximate arbitrary authority frameworks, and this approximation can be done by considering frameworks with the same order and size.
A new type of shadow framework, called a framework of authority and anti-authority, is defined, and this is characterized by the absence of a certain type of subgraph called a frame.
This new framework can be used to approximate arbitrary authority frameworks, and this approximation can be done by considering frameworks with the same order and size.
The framework of authority and anti-authority is used to prove two new results.
One result proves that two authority frameworks are equivalent if and only if they are identical, and this proof relies on the fact that any two authority frameworks can be embedded into a framework of authority and anti-authority.
